In evaluating the effectiveness of a cancer treatment, tumor samples must be analyzed for the presence of infiltrating lymphocytes and their cell types.  While deep learning-based methods have excelled in categorizing these cells in image datasets, there are significant challenges in applying such methods directly to medical labs.  These challenges include the need for a centralized image database and the risk of data contamination.  To address these issues, a new approach is proposed that utilizes a federated approach to deep learning.  In this approach, a global model is trained that can identify tumor regions on images from multiple participating medical labs without the need for a centralized database.  The proposed system is tested with four participating labs and shows a high level of consistency in classifying lymphocytes and cell types against a pre-trained baseline model that had access to a centralized database.  The code for the proposed system is also made available on GitHub.  In particular, the system is able to classify lymphocytes with a consistency of 92% against a baseline that had access to a centralized database.  The proposed system is also compared to other deep learning-based approaches that were trained on a centralized database and shows a high level of consistency in classifying cell types such as macrophages, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.  The system is designed to reduce the burden on medical labs by only requiring the transmission of tumor region masks and achieving a high level of performance that is comparable to models that were trained on a centralized database.  The proposed system also has potential applications in other medical imaging challenges that involve the classification of rare cell types.  The challenges and solutions described in this paper can also inform the broader ML4H community about the possibilities and challenges of applying ML in a medical lab setting.  The paper is presented at the ML4H workshop that is organized in conjunction with the International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention (MICCAI). In this study, a well-known issue in fiber-optic communications is highlighted, specifically the propagation of large errors that can impede the performance of Decision-Feedback Equalizers (DFEs). To address this challenge, a new DFE structure called the Partial Sample-Restoration DFE (PSRDFE) is presented and tested over a 40 Gb/s submarine fiber-optic link. During a 24-hour field trial, the PSRDFE exhibited enhanced throughput and reduced bit error rates compared to conventional DFEs. Analysis and numerical experiments have validated the superior performance of the PSRDFE. This study provides valuable insights into the complex interplay of fiber nonlinearity, polarization-mode dispersion, and sampling errors that affect DFEs. To circumvent these challenges, the PSRDFE employs counter-propagating pilot signals to counter polarization-mode dispersion and sampling errors, and incorporates a more efficient error-correcting algorithm. Through the conversion of time-domain signals, the PSRDFE also facilitates more efficient equalization. With its optimized performance, the PSRDFE has the potential to enhance DFE performance in a variety of fiber-optic communications scenarios. This study also highlights the limitations of DFEs in certain applications and the benefits of alternative equalization techniques, coherent detection, and spectral-slice reception. These findings, in turn, inform strategies for optimizing the sampling period, delay lines, and trellis depth of DFEs in real-world deployments. To further improve DFEs, research into more effective error-propagation mitigation strategies is also advocated. To this end, a novel, simplified model for predicting the performance of DFEs has been developed and is presented. This new framework for analyzing the behavior of DFEs in the field will provide a valuable tool for designing and optimizing these components for real-world communications applications. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. However, these models can be memory-intensive and computationally costly, mainly due to their heavy, unoptimized parameter structure. Our innovative Pruning In Time (PIT) framework addresses this challenge by incorporating a set of optimizations specifically designed to streamline TCNs across both time and feature dimensions. PIT combines element-wise and filter-wise pruning strategies to minimize unnecessary computations and reduce memory requirements. Furthermore, PIT introduces a new, efficient initialization method aimed at balancing model performance and sparsity. By harnessing the capabilities of both linear and sparse TCNs, PIT provides a versatile and effective solution for deploying lightweight and high-performance TCNs on resource-constrained devices. Experimental results across various datasets and models demonstrate the efficacy of PIT in achieving a suitable balance between performance and sparsity. Compared to existing pruning methods, PIT yields improved performance under the same sparsity level or enhanced performance with higher sparsity levels, thus making it an ideal solution for a wide range of embedded ML applications. Moreover, our work showcases the versatility of PIT by successfully applying it to a range of TCN-based models employed for time-series classification, including TCNs, Graph Convolutional Networks, and Document Classification Networks. The source code of the PIT framework is publicly available on the Pit4TCN GitHub repository. With the rapid growth of time-series data generation, the need for efficient and lightweight TCNs has never been more pressing. By pioneering a new approach to TCN optimization, PIT has set a high bar for future research to strive for even greater heights. This letter presents first-time measurements of transverse flow angle and flow magnitude fluctuations in lead-lead collisions at a 5.02 TeV collision energy, obtained using a method that mitigates global elliptic flow uncertainty. The measurements were conducted for various centralities and revealed smaller kurtosis values for the flow angle distribution compared to the flow magnitude distribution. Furthermore, the ratio of flow magnitude to flow angle kurtosis exhibited dependence on initial condition anisotropy, flow resistance, and viscosity-to-entropy ratio, providing new insights into the complex interplay between these factors in heavy-ion collisions. Additionally, the findings for the ratio of flow magnitude to flow angle skewness showed dependence on flow resistance and viscosity-to-entropy ratio, offering a better understanding of the viscous behavior of quark-gluon plasma. These findings, derived from lead-lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, contribute valuable information to the ongoing study of heavy-ion collisions.

We present new findings from the spectroscopic analysis of Tonantzintla 2, a metal-poor globular cluster located in the Milky Way's central bulge. Disregarding Tonantzintla 2's contamination and using APOGEE data, we determined the cluster's parameters including its radial velocity, orbit, and atmospheric properties. The results indicate a spherical cluster with an almost circular orbit around the galaxy. Tonantzintla 2's members exhibit a range of metal contents [-1.08, -0.75]. We discovered a previously unknown population in the cluster zone and estimated its abundance based on [Ca II] line measurements from APOGEE spectra, confirming the cluster's metal-poor nature. The cluster's light consists of 57% red giants and 43% upper sub-giant branches. Its distribution is bi-modal, reflecting the bi-modal distribution of red giants in the cluster. We observed a gap of 0.25 days in the rotation period distribution of red giants in Tonantzintla 2. The cluster's unique features, low metal content, and distinct light curve make it an ideal target for studying the rotation period variable red giants in the galaxy's bulge. The data also reveal a greater abundance of the light element carbon in Tonantzintla 2 compared to other metal-poor clusters. The cluster's carbon enhancement is attributed to the destruction of hydrogen shells in its small, compact giant stars. The enhanced carbon in Tonantzintla 2 may result from the cluster's historical interaction with the galaxy's bulge. The cluster's past encounter with the bulge's dense field left it with a higher carbon content, a feature shared by the cluster's upper sub-giant branch. The enhanced carbon in Tonantzintla 2 is confirmed by the rotation period variable red giants' faster rotation at higher latitudes, a feature caused by the cluster's irregular shape. A massive arc, dubbed PXB-1, was identified in the PV sky model, exhibiting a significant excess in signal across multiple frequency bands.  Analyzing this feature with the PV sky model and a physical lens model, we determined that it is not a traditional arc formed by a bright background source, but rather a distorted image of a massive background galaxy, GJ 3337-G.  This galaxy is highly irregular and lies at a redshift of approximately 0.022, about 90 Mpc directly in front of the Milky Way.  Based on observations from the ATLAS K-band atlas and the 2MASS fluxes, GJ 3337-G exhibits characteristics of an irregular spiral galaxy similar to the Milky Way, with a mass estimated at over 10^11 solar masses.  Furthermore, we found that this galaxy is not detectable in radio observations, likely due to its large distance.  Therefore, the most reliable determination of its mass is through the lensing effect on the arc, where the mass of the lens, the lensing effect, and the source galaxy's brightness form a self-consistent picture.  This discovery opens up new perspectives for finding massive foreground galaxies by analyzing traditional arcs in lens systems.  In the case of PXB-1, the lens is an massive early-type galaxy located in the Virgo cluster, and by analyzing the arc in this system, we found the lens to be a massive galaxy with a mass of over 10^11 solar masses at a redshift of 0.056.  This finding also highlights the usefulness of combining lens models with sky models to identify hidden sources, a technique that can be applied to upcoming sensitive CMB experiments like Simons Observatory and CMB-S4.  By utilizing these experiments' ability to detect subtle lens effects, we can determine the mass of lens galaxies at high redshifts, providing new insights into the distribution of mass in the universe. To overcome these challenges, we've developed novel, high-efficiency algorithms for estimating backdoors, confounders, causal effects, and noise models, which can be combined into the Causal Exploration Toolbox. This toolbox allows for an efficient discovery of causal structures, models, and functions among multiple variables, with both theoretical and practical guarantees, as demonstrated by our experiments on both synthetic and real-world data. The Causal Exploration Toolbox is an open-source framework that can be used in conjunction with the PAC-Bayes-SDM framework, which provides an upper bound for the expected error of our predictions in terms of computational resources. Furthermore, the toolbox is compatible with both Bayesian and frequentist settings. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs when the sphere's surface breaks through the water's tension. As it enters the water, the sphere creates an air cavity, and surface seal happens when this cavity is closed off. Researchers have attempted to analyze this phenomenon by observing the spheres as they enter the water at various speeds, and our findings reveal that changing the sphere's velocity affects the size of the air cavity created. A velocity range exists, often called the medium velocity range, where changing the sphere's velocity only minimally impacts the size of the cavity. Additionally, our data indicates that increasing the sphere's velocity within this middle range results in a smaller cavity, and water splashing during this process follows a pattern often called a "splash ring". A theoretical model has been developed to better understand how the sphere's velocity affects the size of the air cavity and the splash ring. Constructive interference is proposed to explain the rosette shape of the splash ring, and factors such as water pressure, air pressure, and the sphere's velocity all contribute to the size of the air cavity. A dimensionless plot has been created to display how the sphere's velocity impacts the size of the air cavity and the splash ring. This research builds upon earlier studies on this topic, and the middle velocity range exists because the splash ring patterns become too complex to predict at higher speeds. The data and models presented provide a foundation for further exploration of this phenomenon. The models have been validated through both numerical analysis and first-hand observations of the spheres entering the water at various speeds, and the developed theoretical model can be applied to spheres entering other fluids. The study of this phenomenon may also offer insights for improving the surface seal performance of spheres in motion. The research presented and the models developed are applicable across various sphere sizes, though only spheres with diameters ranging from 50 to 75 millimeters were directly studied. Spheres with diameters outside of this range range may behave differently due to factors such as increased air resistance at higher velocities, though the underlying principles of surface seal should still apply. The study of these phenomena can also provide insights for improving the performance of spheres in motion, and the models presented are a step in that direction. In order to safeguard against malicious hardware attacks like Spectre and Meltdown, hardware components are being isolated from one another using hardware-based isolation techniques such as SANITIZEd. However, implementing and maintaining such hardware components can be very expensive. This research aims to minimize the reliance on such expensive hardware by re-architecting system hardware components with side-channel attacks in mind, thus enabling the safe sharing of physically adjacent hardware. A hardware component called SafeZone has been designed and tested as a part of this research. SafeZone is a processing unit with a limited capacity for execution, designed to run untrusted code, thereby minimizing the risk of malicious hardware attacks on critical system components. This research also presents a prototype called Minisafe, built using the SafeZone hardware component, to demonstrate its effectiveness. In Minisafe, the SafeZone unit is responsible for executing unverified code and managing memory, while the main CPU, isolated from physical contamination, runs verified code and manages system memory. This research demonstrates that Minisafe can successfully prevent malicious hardware attacks like Spectre and Meltdown, and also reduces memory errors caused by hardware corruption, without incurring any performance overhead. Furthermore, Minisafe is cost-effective, with a price that is half as much as a system that uses expensive hardware-based isolation techniques. This research is particularly relevant to embedded systems and mobile devices with limited resources, and also presents a cost-effective solution for mitigating malicious hardware attacks in mainstream desktop and laptop computers. This research has been showcased as a demo at the EuroSys 2019 conference, and the source code of Minisafe has been made available on GitHub, featuring a demonstration of malicious hardware attacks on a Minisafe system using the Address Space Isolation technique. Furthermore, the VentEnhance code is shared publicly to encourage the development of more advanced ventilator enhancement strategies. In this paper, the term "dynamic enhancement" refers to the conversion of a single mechanical ventilator into a dual-patient ventilator setup with the aid of pharmacological neuromuscular blockade. This "Ventenhance" technique leverages optimal control and the specific physiology of each patient to safely and effectively treat two patients with a single ventilator. This issue was modeled using a ventenhance variational inequality (VVI) formulation, and a key aspect of this paper is the explicit discussion of the Ventenhance formulation. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently feature complex geological structures that make static and dynamic reservoir modeling challenging. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering, guided by up-to-date models of the subsurface. These models must be constructed from regularly obtained well log data, which necessitates the development of efficient static modeling tools that can handle a large volume of data. Given the uncertainty inherent in geosteering, it's essential to employ modeling tools that acknowledge and quantify uncertainties to minimize risks and optimize placement for hydrocarbon recovery. This study presents a novel, ensemble-based static modeling approach that utilizes a range of techniques, including smoothie, compact neural networks, and generative adversarial networks, to build models and estimate uncertainties from well log data. This approach was applied to real well log data from the North Sea, with results showing it can create realistic models and quantify uncertainties effectively. Further, this approach was tested and validated for geosteering, with the study demonstrating that real-time application can lead to accurate and reliable results in complex offshore reservoirs. This approach was also found to be more robust and efficient compared to conventional approaches using neural networks and ensemble methods. This work has implications for the broader oil and gas industry, with potential to be applied in other reservoirs and geosteering scenarios. The existence of an undiscovered planet, often referred to as Planet X, has been hypothesized based on the irregular orbit of Sedna, a remote dwarf planet in the outer reaches of the solar system. Computer simulations predicting its presence suggest the planet could weigh up to 22 Earth masses and maintain a highly elongated, 800-year orbital path. Planet X is believed to exert a gravitational impact on the Kuiper Belt, causing the slightly displaced orientation of the unique asteroid 2005 CD 19. However, detecting the influence of this planet on the known orbiting bodies in the solar system is more complicated and might be hidden by the existing level of astrophysical noise. Using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo analysis and current orbital data for the outer planets, we find that the existing gravitational influence of Planet X cannot be distinguished from the noise in the data available since 1970. A significant improvement in the accuracy of the planetary orbits, specifically for Neptune, would be necessary to increase the signal-to-noise ratio by a factor of about 10, potentially allowing the detection of the Planet X effect by around 2027. Until then, the existence of the hidden world will remain in the dark. The required accuracy for detecting the Planet X effect on the orbital path of Neptune could be met by around 2025. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining popularity as various online services generate rich user data across multiple platforms. However, most existing methods are limited by their single-domain sparsity issue, which hinders the effectiveness of recommended results. To address this problem, we introduce a novel multi-sparse-domain cooperative framework, where each domain is treated as an independent aspect with its own unique characteristics. By incorporating an enhanced comprehensive aspect preference learning method, we develop a unified representation for all aspects, allowing for joint learning and a collaborative filter technique. Furthermore, we propose an aspect-specific adaptation module to remedy the differences in data quality across domains, thus ensuring that each aspect makes a fair contribution to the overall model. Our experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our recommended results over state-of-the-art cross-domain recommendation methods. Additionally, we observe the practical applicability of our model in a real-world e-commerce scenario. Our open-source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zheng-hao/ECAPL. Prior studies attempting to substitute human assessments with automatic models have focused on resolving a single issue - either handling inter-site variations or accommodating diverse pathology - but the complexity of the problem extends further, given the numerous factors influencing image quality. This work redefines the challenge, recognizing that any effective solution must account for differences between specific MRI configurations, variations in tissue contrasts, and distinct types of anatomical abnormalities, all while ensuring the model's ability to generalize across these factors. A cutting-edge ConvNeXt-based model was developed and validated on a substantial, diverse dataset containing over 20,000 scored MRI slices from six distinct sites, encompassing various configurations and multiple types of soft-tissue pathologies. The foundation theorem is a significant concept in the theory of Coxeter groups, particularly in the area of Coxeter geometry. It has far-reaching implications, connecting the geometry of a Coxeter group to its order, and has been extensively explored in the context of finite Coxeter groups. However, its development is hindered by the limitation that Coxeter spaces must be simplicial, which creates an obstacle when studying complex reflection arrays. The foundation theorem is particularly relevant to the generalized Coxeter groups, and we extend the foundation theorem to these groups, removing the requirement that Coxeter spaces be simplicial. Moreover, we establish a connection between the foundation theorem and the order of the generalized Coxeter groups. The order of these groups can be determined using the foundation theorem by analyzing the dimensions of their fundamental chambers. Additionally, we identify the underlying rationale for the foundation theorem over the real numbers, and we establish an interesting link between the foundation theorem and the concept of the Coxeter polytopes. Using the Pantheon supernova dataset and a weak lensing map from the DES, we perform a cosmological analysis by combining Type Ia supernovae and cosmic shear data. We apply a lensing weight calculation to the supernoviae based on their angular positions, effectively amplifying their signal by up to 30\% in the analysis. This approach allows for a coherent analysis of supernovae and cosmic shear, rather than analyzing these phenomena in separate steps. 

Regardless of the analysis method, we find similar tensions between our results and the DES's assumed cosmological parameters. Specifically, our amplification analysis of the supernovae dataset yields a lower Hubble constant value of $H_0 = 67.5 \pm 3.2$ km/s/Mpc, as opposed to the $H_0 = 68.8 \pm 0.5$ km/s/Mpc reported by the DES. This discrepancy persists even when accounting for potential supernovae sample selection effects. 

By comparing different supernovae samples, we identify a bias in the Pantheon dataset that favors shorter look-back times, which could mask the Hubble constant tension. This preference is less pronounced in the more restricted and homogeneous DES-SN dataset. 

Ultimately, our study highlights the significance of considering potential correlations between supernovae and cosmic shear when analyzing these phenomena together, which may lead to biased interpretations of the data. 

Based on our analysis, we derive a new constraint for the matter density parameter $\Omega_m = 0.26 \pm 0.04$ by combining the amplified Type Ia supernovae with cosmic shear. This estimate is consistent with the DES's findings for $\Omega_m$, albeit with a wider confidence interval.

These are lecture notes for a 6-hour mini-course on stochastic partial differential equations presented at the University of Oxford in April-May 2021. 

The main objective of these lecture notes is to provide an in-depth explanation of the stochastic Navier-Stokes equations by first introducing the necessary concepts from probability and partial differential equations. 

The first chapter covers the fundamental principles of probability measures, especially focusing on the Borel-Cantelli-Lebesgue theorem, and the associated Borel-Cantelli probabilities. 

The second chapter explores the concept of independent increments, starting with the definition of independence, Poisson random measures, and eventually leading to Ito Brownian motion and its properties. 

The third chapter delves into the theory of deterministic linear partial differential equations with unique solutions, specifically addressing existence, uniqueness, and continuous dependence on initial conditions and data. 

The fourth chapter builds upon previous concepts to analyze the existence, uniqueness, and dependence on data of stochastic partial differential equations. 

The fifth chapter is an overview of different types of noise, including deterministic, bounded, and unbounded noise, and their respective applications to SPDEs.

MRI technology utilizes radio waves to obtain non-invasive images of the inside of the body, specifically to visualize tumors for accurate diagnosis and treatment. This study focuses on enhancing the performance of image processing using edge detection methods, specifically the Canny operator, and analyzing key characteristics of tumors. Although edge detection can be a powerful tool, it is vulnerable to noise and inconsistencies common in MRI images. To mitigate these issues, this study employs mathematical operations to enhance the image clarity and precision. The aim is to develop a more effective image processing algorithm capable of precisely identifying and differentiating tumors in MRI images. 

For this investigation, PASCAL VOC 2010 and a custom dataset were utilized as reference standards for training and testing the algorithm. The proposed algorithm consists of the following components:
1. Preprocessing: to enhance image clarity.
2. Canny edge detection: to identify and differentiate tumor edges from the surrounding area.
4. Region-based segmentation: to split the image into distinct regions based on gray scale values.
5. Merge and refine: to combine and refine the results from edge detection and region-based segmentation.

The proposed algorithm was evaluated using precision, recall, and F-score metrics. Compared to existing methods, our results show an enhanced performance in precision, recall, and F-score. Furthermore, our study reveals that edge detection plays a crucial role in tumor identification, while region-based segmentation contributes to accurate differentiation. Additionally, we observed that edge detection is more effective in detecting irregular tumor shapes, whereas region-based segmentation is more efficient in identifying tumors with clear boundaries. 

In conclusion, this investigation highlights the effectiveness of combining edge detection and region-based segmentation in tumor identification and differentiation. This study may serve as a foundation for further exploration of image processing using edge detection in medical diagnostics. Nonetheless, more comprehensive research is necessary to validate these findings on a broader population. As for the field of medical diagnostics through image processing, future studies could examine the application of edge detection in radiography, ultrasound, and CT scans. Additionally, there is a potential for researchers to delve into the use of edge detection in analyzing multiple types of tumors and in developing automated tumor detection systems.

These implicit ties can be discovered in various contexts, including on-line interactions, biological connections, and latent categories. They may represent meaningful patterns or functional groups, making it essential to identify them for both practical and theoretical purposes. This paper introduces an unsupervised and explicit framework for discovering implicit ties, where connections are identified based on their uniqueness and relevance within a given context. A set of unsupervised filters is used to refine the implicit ties and associate them with underlying features or functions, and a method for meaningful tie naming is proposed, leveraging both natural language processing and human feedback, to create more accurate and understandable labels. The effectiveness of this framework is demonstrated through the identification of implicit groups, functions, and semantic relationships in various datasets and scenarios. Furthermore, the framework is shown to be adaptable for use cases involving online and offline data, including biological protein connections and online community networks. The proposed framework is comprised of three primary components: 1) an unsupervised tie extraction method, 2) tie refinement via filtering, and 3) a tie naming system using both human-provided data and automatic predictions. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 20,000 unique terms over a 10-year period, spanning multiple million documents. We demonstrate the inadequacy of these models in capturing the polarities introduced by Loughran and McDonald through a series of explicit experiments, including the development of a binary classification system for identifying polarized terms. This classification system shows little improvement over a chance baseline, yet performs significantly better when compared to a baseline using a bag-of-words representation. We observe the presence of discriminant distributions in our data, and explore potential solutions to enhance the word2vec model to better capture the polarities introduced by Loughran and McDonald, including the incorporation of additional terms and the use of adversarial learning. We believe our work provides a foundation for a deeper understanding of the limitations of the word2vec model and its applications in the field of NLP. As a result of this research, we release an open-source, publicly available implementation of the word2vec model, tailored to the Skip-gram learning method, T-Skipgram, available on GitHub at https://github.com/alegotti/T-Skipgram. We also introduce an executable version of our experiments, available on GitHub at https://github.com/alegotti/Word2Vec-LM. Additionally, we introduce a new dataset, available on GitHub at https://github.com/alegotti/Word2Vec-LM, containing the results of our experiments, including the synthetic corpora, the financial news dataset, and the state-of-the-art implementations of the word2vec model. We hope this work will inspire a deeper examination of the limitations of the word2vec model and its applications in the field of NLP, and we look forward to engaging with the research

Current logical languages lack a practical application due to the absence of unary connectives representing context-dependent discourse, which are vital for achieving a genuine separation between semantic structure and the context in which they are expressed. This issue is addressed by introducing a quantum-based interpretation that utilizes context-dependent spin states to assign meaning to formulas, with the added benefit of providing a foundation for processing multiple contexts at once. A set of uniformly applicable rules for the quantum interpretation is also proposed, drawing from the principles of dLP and the context-shifting functor, and is demonstrated through the development of an executable specification in Isabelle. This execution facilitates the creation of context-dependent models and the generation of context-dependent truth tables with imaginary units. The integration of context-dependent discourse is exemplified through the analysis of an epistemic case study. This work presents an innovative approach to incorporating context-dependent discourse via unary connectives within a quantum logical framework, offering a novel solution to the long-standing issue of context-dependent valuation. This solution allows for context-dependent truth values and provides a foundation for investigating other context-dependent constructs. Furthermore, this work showcases the utility of this approach through a real-world application, providing a framework for developing context-dependent reasoning about epistemic logic and other related disciplines. This approach is also shown to be executable and verifiable within the Isabelle/HOL platform. This work is a stepping stone for addressing more complex context-dependent issues and expanding the scope of application beyond epistemic logic. This work is a part of a broader research on context-dependent constructs and our findings can be seen as an answer to the open problem posed by the authors in the context of dLP. This library provides an efficient and straightforward way for experts and non-experts alike to perform exact diagonalizations on quantum systems by transforming a high-level language into a usable form for diagonalization. Each operator in the system is defined using a simple, intuitive syntax derived from the commutator algebra, which allows for the exact diagonalization of multiple quantum systems, including spin, fermion, boson, and qubit models, using a variety of algorithms, including the Lanczos method, by casting them as commuting sub-domains. Furthermore, libcommute has been ported to Python 3 as pycommute, which maintains the core features and precision of its C++ parent, while also providing a more user-friendly interface and an easy-to-use GUI for defining models and diagonalizing them. Establishing a reliable connection between the electronic structure and the superconducting gap structure in iron-based superconductors still presents a significant challenge and would require a more comprehensive understanding derived from multiple first-principles calculations, including authentic band structure, charge density, and superconducting gap structure. In this study, we examine the electronic and structural properties of (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ using first-principles methods with accurate starting conditions, and our results show a consistent match with experimental data, including magnetic moments, lattice parameters, and charge density distribution. Notably, our calculations yield a $s$+$d$-wave mixed superconducting gap structure, which is in line with earlier theoretical models. This finding is validated by our results for the superconducting gap structure on the Fe and As sites, which display the "hole-like" and "electron-like" characteristics, respectively. Our analysis also highlights the relevance of spin-orbit coupling in iron-based superconductors, and we observe the asymmetrical distribution of superconducting gap values on the Fe and As sites. These results provide a solid theoretical foundation for understanding the intricate relationship between the electronic structure, superconducting gap structure, and material properties in (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$. Moreover, our analysis suggests that the local spin-orbit coupling could serve as a key factor in determining the superconducting gap structure in iron-based superconductors. Additionally, we propose that the As-resonance observed in angular resolved photoemission spectroscopy, which is a crucial piece of evidence for $s$+$d$-wave superconductivity, can be interpreted as a result of the superconducting gap values being greater on the Fe sites than on the As sites. Our results demonstrate that the authentic electronic structure and superconducting gap structure of (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ can be accurately understood through first-principles calculations, providing a valuable framework for investigating other iron-based superconductors. Furthermore, we suggest that local field shielding effects could contribute to the material's high superconducting transition temperatures observed in iron-based superconductors. Our study offers a valuable framework for investigating other iron-based superconductors, and it highlights the significance of taking the spin-orbit coupling into account when analyzing the superconducting gap structure

A comprehensive study of the metal-insulator transition in LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices is presented, utilizing $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR for in-depth analysis.  LaNiO$_3$ is a representative of the unusual metallic state observed in rare-earth perovskite systems with no nearby magnetic impurities, despite being next to a Mott insulator on the phase diagram.  A detailed examination of the spin-lattice relaxation mechanism indicates that the Li NMR signal is directly coupled to the Ni valence, allowing the study of spin dynamics across the metal-insulator transition.  The observed changes in the NMR spectra as the transition is approached are indicative of increased spin fluctuations in the metal state.  The results provide direct evidence for the involvement of Ni valence in the metal-insulator transition and offer a new perspective on the underlying physics governing this phenomenon, supporting the model of valence fluctuality.  The study of spin dynamics in the Li NMR spectra reveals two distinct components, a fast fluctuating local moment associated with the Ni site and a more slowly fluctuating moment with a longer correlation time, linked to the movement of the electron wave packet across the superlattice.  The possibility of the Li NMR to probe different components of the electronic state makes it a versatile tool for the investigation of transition metal superlattices.  The study of the Li NMR spectra across the metal-insulator transition reveals a more intricate picture than previously observed with other methods, showing distinct changes in the spectral weight as the transition is approached and offering new insights into the physics governing this phenomenon.  The results presented in this study provide a new framework for the understanding of rare-earth perovskite systems and the effects of interface coupling in superlattices. Effective dialogue models are crucial for our increasingly conversation-driven society, and it's essential to develop assessment tools that push the boundaries of complexity in dialogue interactions. Current evaluation benchmarks, such as the MultiWOZ 2.0, are limited by their simple tree structures, which underrepresent the complexities encountered in real-life conversations. To address this shortcoming, we present MultiTalk, a new evaluation benchmark that features highly branched dialogue trees, making it especially challenging for current state-of-the-art models to achieve high scores. MultiTalk includes 1,578 distinct topic branches, spanning over 12 topically diverse categories and incorporates a total of 20,015 conversation turns. Unlike previous benchmarks, it employs a more human-centered approach to topic definitions and structure, using a method that prioritizes natural language processing aspects. To demonstrate the efficacy of MultiTalk, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation of seven different model ensembles, using various performance metrics and incorporating human evaluation as well. The results show significant performance gaps between current state-of-the-art models and the challenges posed by MultiTalk, indicating a clear path for future research and advancements in the field. To integrate genomic data and genome-wide association studies, we used a combination of functional genomics and physical chromatin structure to organize the human genome into 182 distinct functional units. We then analyzed 18 different trait datasets using a variety of approaches, including expression quantitative trait studies, chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing, and genome-wide association studies. Our method effectively pinpointed significant associations within each trait, even when no prior knowledge was available. For example, we found a strong connection between enhancer regions and the genetics of blood cell counts, and we identified a large number of associated genes with type 2 diabetes through the examination of promoter regions and chromatin structure. Our approach is suitable for a wide range of applications and we make available a public database that includes detailed information on protein-coding regions, noncoding regions, and phenotypic traits in humans. Additionally, we conducted a comprehensive assessment of our approach using artificial data, and it showed that it is an effective way to identify relevant genetic variations associated with a given trait. Our study also involved a large number of collaborators from the ENCODE and GWAS consortia.

Observations of the Galactic Centre have revealed a substantial number of low-luminosity X-ray binaries in quiescence, which are likely powered by neutron stars instead of black holes as previously assumed. It has been hypothesized that these neutron star binaries enter a transient state powered by an accretion process, emitting intense X-ray radiation from a source such as an X-ray binary. However, determining the duration of these transients is crucial, as it would allow us to pinpoint the source and account for the entire energy output. A recent study published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society investigated the time intervals between X-ray outbursts from neutron star binaries, incorporating new data from the MAXI/Telescope and the ASAS-SN optical telescope. 

By analyzing a comprehensive dataset spanning nearly 2 decades with nearly 1000 days of coverage, researchers discovered a distinct distribution of recurrence intervals, which peaks at approximately 20 years for neutron star binaries that exhibit outburst patterns similar to those of the low-mass X-ray binary binary, GRU J1657.03-3759. 

However, a distinct subgroup with significantly shorter median recurrence intervals of about 2.5 years was also identified. Recent advances in conversational AI have been driven by large language models trained on natural language inference tasks, which emphasize categorical judgments about semantic relationships. However, the underlying assumptions of these models have not been thoroughly examined. Our study explores the diversity of semantics present in real conversations and infers the presuppositions underlying popular NLI datasets. We find that these datasets largely focus on explicitly stated facts but neglect implicit semantic concepts. Additionally, we investigate the diversity of semantics in conversations and identify numerous rich, often implicitly expressed ideas. These underlying semantics can be distinct from the explicit statements made by users. We also examine the variety of semantics present in NLI datasets, which we believe results in conversational AI models developed from these datasets being prone to selecting safe, obvious answers over more meaningful, engaging ones. Our findings suggest that evaluating the diversity of semantics is essential when assessing the performance of these models. We support this claim by demonstrating that models optimized to perform well on NLI datasets but neglecting semantic variety fail to engage users in natural conversations. In contrast, they perform equally as well on tasks requiring them to respond safely and accurately. Our study provides concrete datasets and statistical analysis to guide the development of more versatile conversational AI models. These models not only safely respond to user queries but also have the capacity to explore new topics and express their own opinions. We believe our work is relevant to individuals interested in advancing the art of conversation, including those working on related topics such as topic variety, engaging versus safe conversations, and the challenging task of human-computer dialogue evaluation. We hope our study to be a useful reference for researchers exploring these research questions and seek to collaborate with them. Furthermore, we develop a novel dataset containing labeled diversity data, which can be used to train models to generate more varied responses. We leverage this data to train models that prioritize diversity over performance on NLI tasks and evaluate their performance against models trained with standard self-supervised objectives. Our results demonstrate that models trained with diversity in mind are better equipped to engage users in natural conversations and infer the underlying semantics of NLI datasets. A major safety issue with automated driving systems is their inability to accurately predict and prevent hazardous situations, particularly when other vehicles are involved.  In an effort to address this challenge, a deep learning-based recognition system for hazardous actions during lane changes has been proposed. Recent advancements in computer architecture have achieved remarkable improvements, yet the evolution of CPU frequencies has slowed significantly over the past decade. To fully take advantage of these advancements, using multiple frequencies within a chip has become a prevalent technique. However, controlling and adjusting these frequencies in real-time introduces two major challenges: the need for a high-speed controller and the potential for increased power consumption. We have developed a novel, lower-cost and high-efficiency solution, where a simple controller employs a random sampling technique to determine when to switch frequencies. Our proposed method, HyperDegrade, was tested on a state-of-the-art CPU and the results show it can achieve a 1.6x improvement in energy efficiency and a 1.5x increase in performance, all while maintaining below 10% performance variability. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of HyperDegrade on multi-threaded applications and we believe it has the potential to be an energy-efficient solution for controlling frequency switching. We have open-sourced HyperDegrade on a commercial CPU and are exploring the possibility of collaborating with industry partners to integrate this technology into production-grade processors. With proper design, a 32-core CPU featuring HyperDegrade could potentially achieve a 2.5x improvement in energy efficiency. We have also developed a lower-cost, smaller HyperDegrade variant called HyperDegrade-L, which could be integrated into edge computing devices to improve their performance and energy efficiency. The results of HyperDegrade-L show a 2x improvement in energy efficiency and a 2x increase in performance, all while maintaining below 10% performance variability. The development of HyperDegrade-L has sparked our interest in exploring more complex degradation strategies and we have open-sourced the HyperDegrade-L framework on a popular open-source SoC platform. We have also developed a new degradation strategy called HyperDegrade-S, which features a more complex switching pattern and has shown a 2.5x improvement in energy efficiency and a 2.5x increase in performance, all while maintaining below 10% performance variability. The results of HyperDegrade-S have sparked our interest in exploring this technique on other types of processing elements and we have open-sourced the HyperDegrade-S framework on a popular open-source GPU platform. We have investigated the applicability of HyperDegrade-S to CPUs and found that it can achieve a 2x improvement in energy efficiency and a 2x increase in performance, all while maintaining below 10% performance variability.

This paper examines the privacy issues associated with Federated Learning, particularly in a vertical FL setup where participants train a model using their local data and contribute to a larger model across multiple parties. Our analysis highlights the potential for a privacy breach when a single participant shares model information with the server, as it may lead to inferring sensitive information from that participant. Our main finding reveals that, in a vertical FL context, an adversary-controlled server can effectively recover highly precise information about a participant's dataset even when the model is trained with a robust differential privacy implementation. This breach holds true for various datasets, including categorical and numerical data, as well as when the participant's dataset includes free-text data. Moreover, our results demonstrate that differential privacy offers limited protection to a participant's dataset even when the model is trained with an enhanced privacy-enhancing transformation. Consequently, our analysis advocates for the incorporation of explicit privacy protection measures for participants in a vertical FL setup. To this end, we propose a practical application of homomorphic encryption to safeguard a participant's private data, as evidenced by a substantially increased breach cost for the adversary. This leads to an increased computational overhead for the participant but ensures robust protection for their dataset. This homomorphic encryption approach can be integrated with existing differential privacy implementations through a suitable transformation of the model parameters. This resulting system provides a secure and private learning framework for a vertical FL setup. This research is an initial foray into analyzing the practical privacy challenges of a vertical FL setup, and future work is anticipated to explore the practical challenges of horizontal FL in depth. Kernel methods have proven highly effective for various machine learning tasks, yet their scalability to large datasets is limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise computations. A widely adopted technique to increase kernel method scalability is random feature mapping, which approximates a kernel using a linear transformation and replaces costly pairwise computations with efficient dot product operations. Although this approach has been successfully applied in several contexts, its effectiveness is heavily dependent on an appropriate choice of kernel and dimensionality reduction method. This paper proposes a novel two-stage approach for kernel approximation, known as kernel feature mapping, which first estimates the kernel based on the dataset at hand and then employs this estimated kernel for dimensionality reduction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to support vector machine classification and semi-supervised regression, using synthetic and real-world datasets. Notably, our results indicate that our approach surpasses the efficacy of traditional random feature mapping methods in many cases. We also investigate the characteristics of our proposed kernel estimates and provide insights into their behavior across varying dataset properties. Furthermore, we make our implementation publicly available to facilitate reproducibility and usability. This approach is particularly useful for datasets with unique patterns or structures that are not captured by traditional kernel methods. We anticipate that our findings will be of utility to researchers working on enhanced methods for data-dependent kernel approximation. Additionally, we explore the integration of our proposed approach with transfer learning and weighted kernel methods, which hold promise for further improving the efficacy of kernel-based machine learning models. This study tackles one major challenge in trapped-ion quantum computing - achieving precise and stable rotation operations around the motionless qubits. To overcome this hurdle, we've developed an efficient gate technique, inspired by the Molmer-Sorensen sequence, which utilizes balanced combinations of multiple harmonic modes to create a stable and uniform "rotating frame" of reference. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in multiple trap environments, and we've established a principle for optimizing the performance of this gate method, even when there are fluctuations in the motion characteristics. We've successfully executed this gate technique on the $^{40}$K$^{+}$ ion, with a total of three available motional modes, and our results show that this method can generate a stable period-1 M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate with a minimum error of 1.3$\%$ under ideal conditions, and 4.6$\%$ when considering the fluctuations in motion, without the need for initial state preparations or precise calibration of the laser frequency. Furthermore, we've analyzed the potential for this gate method to be combined with other gate techniques to achieve high-fidelity quantum processing.

Rate data, often represented as a ratio or proportion, are just as important as count data, which are typically expressed as a number or quantity. Unfortunately, current statistical methods fail to acknowledge the interdependence of these two dimensions, doing so would allow for a more comprehensive exploration of binomial distributions. Our proposed framework, CRM (short for "both quantity and ratio matter"), is an evolution of the traditional binomial distribution that accounts for both success/failure counts and associated rates/proportions. As a result, CRM is suitable for analyzing count data accompanied by rate data in various contexts, including frequency counts, means/means differences, and correlations. Moreover, CRM is highly adaptable and can be applied across multiple platforms, including dedicated R tools and general-purpose programming languages like Python and R Language variants. A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-containment facilities must meet stringent safety standards to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These rooms are equipped with advanced, highly sensitive, and expensive safety systems to achieve this level of containment. Our research reveals a novel risk to NPR containment, one that originates from an unexpected source: sound waves generated by loud music. We experimented with releasing aerosolized SARS-CoV-2 into a negative pressure room equipped with sound waves produced by loud music, and our findings showed a significant increase in viral spread beyond the containment area compared to a silent environment. The magnitude of this increase varied based on several factors, including sound intensity, room size, and airflow patterns. To further explore this discovery, our team designed and built a smaller-scale laboratory chamber to conduct more controlled experiments. These experiments involved scanning the environment and detecting the viral load in both the contaminated area and outside the containment zone. Our research focuses on identifying the underlying scientific principles governing the behavior of aerosolized viruses in the presence of sound waves, and we anticipate that our findings will be relevant to understanding other biological threats that could spread through the air, such as fungal toxins and prions. Furthermore, our discovery and the design of our laboratory chamber have implications for the development of more cost-effective safety systems in biolabs and infectious-containment facilities. Our research has raised the attention of government agencies and biolab operators, and we are currently working with them to implement the design of our laboratory chamber in biodecontamination research at a larger scale. Additionally, our research is being used to inform the development of new safety protocols in biolabs and infectious-containment facilities. A key challenge in modeling decentralized energy markets involves capturing the benefits of storage through risk-adverse agents. To address this, we utilize a unique risk-averse self-allocation approach of storage, framed within robust optimization to account for uncertainty in energy supply and demand. By leveraging the Fisher information matrix to quantify risk, we derive a robust formulation that determines optimal self-allocation levels, enabling the incorporation of risk-adverse storage into standard power management problems. Through a stochastic reformulation and stochastic approximation methods, we develop an computationally efficient solution for large-scale systems, providing an explicit expression for self-allocation levels and bounding optimal expected losses. Numerical experiments, including simulations of various renewable-based scenarios, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in capturing the benefits of storage and improving market performance. As an additional outcome, we observe our method for self-allocation levels generalizes to other applications of robust optimization. Additionally, we investigate how our approach can be integrated with existing market mechanisms and find it yields superior performance in comparison to conventional methods, leading to greater social welfare and more efficient use of storage resources. The vast majority of convolutional neural networks are trained using distillation, which involves training a smaller network to mimic a larger, existing network. This technique is widely employed due to its effectiveness in scaling up neural network training across large image datasets such as ImageNet. However, the traditional approach to distillation has a significant limitation: it relies on fixed knowledge sources, which are often represented by the outputs of a single, frozen network. This assumption is challenged in our research, where we introduce a dynamic learning framework that recognizes knowledge as constantly evolving over time. This framework involves utilizing multiple temporal networks that represent the source and the target, with each being updated dynamically as training progresses. Our proposed method, which leverages dynamic temporal distillation, offers a more accurate representation of the complexities involved in deep neural network training. This is demonstrated through comprehensive evaluations on the CIFAR and ImageNet datasets, where our method outperforms conventional distillation methods across all setting conditions. For instance, our approach yields a remarkable 3.85% reduction in top-1 error on the ImageNet validation set when using ResNet-50, a significant improvement over the existing state of the art. This research provides a theoretical foundation for dynamic learning, which is a promising direction for future research. In addition, our method has been made available as an open-source repository, enabling seamless scalability of neural network training across the ImageNet scale. This is achieved through the use of a customized supercomputer architecture, specifically designed for neural network training, which is also outlined in our research. This design, which is based on a modular architecture consisting of multiple host-server configurations, enables effortless scaling up of neural network training across the ImageNet scale. This is further illustrated through the training of multiple large-scale neural networks on the ImageNet dataset. This includes the training of three different models – EfficientNet-B3, B4, and B5 – on a dataset comprising over 14 billion parameters. This has been accomplished using a customized supercomputer, consisting of 512 GPU nodes, which is also outlined in our research. This has resulted in the lowest known top-1 error rates on the ImageNet validation set to date, with the training of all three models simultaneously. This has led to a further reduction in top-1 error rate of 0.46%. To study donor spins in silicon, we've developed a framework that utilizes effective mass theory to account for interactions between donors by applying a two-dimensional Poisson equation, enabling accurate calculations of donor positions relative to their ground state and first excited state energies. By considering the minimal and heavy electron valley ranges, we've identified suitable configuration options which yield precise results, up to 10 times more efficient than traditional finite element methods. Our approach has been verified by comparing its results to existing experimental data and demonstrates its potential for scaling to study multiple donors with exchange interactions. Our research provides a scientific basis for the development of large-scale donor-based quantum computing systems.

Our investigation focused on the conductance of a quantum point contact, made from HgTe quantum wells, as the magnitude of the applied electric gate varied.  The study began with an examination of the charge carrier structure in HgTe quantum wells, which were shown to transition from hole to electron behavior as the width of the well changed.  The critical widths were identified through magnetotransport measurements and the subsequent analysis of magneto-resistance spectra in relation to the Landau fan diagrams.  The results revealed stable electron accumulation on one side of the quantum contact and a gapless region, which was confirmed by the absence of a classical magnetopetrusitive effect in the narrowest Landau bands.  The investigation further showed that the conductance of the quantum contact displayed an anomalous behavior in comparison to standard two-dimensional systems, characterized by non-quantized plateaus in Landau bands.  The values of transverse conductance were found to be significantly higher than the typical quantized values, which was attributed to the broken symmetry and extra channels provided by the helical zero-energy modes.  The results were verified by integrating the normalized density of states and the corresponding velocity distribution.  The study provides novel insights into the quantum transport of dirac fermions and our findings may be applied to realize robust, symmetric diabatic connections in quantum electronics. In next-generation 5G systems, Dynamic Time Division (TDD) scheduling allows for adaptive management of uplink and downlink transmissions, depending on real-time observations of system state. We propose a new scheduling model that makes decisions at each time slot, aiming to maximize overall throughput while managing interference and ensuring quality of service. This leads to a classic mixed-integer linear programming problem, but because of rapid changes in system state, it's essential to design efficient and distributed algorithms that promote scalability and stability. Building on previous ideas for decentralized scheduling, we create a new algorithm utilizing a generalized version of the Drift-Approximation method, along with a sub-optimal solution that incorporates a new pricing mechanism. This provides a cost-effective solution and improves the performance of previous methods. Simulations show our method to be highly effective in multi-cell systems. Furthermore, we investigate the properties of our method, proving it to be stable and guaranteeing a minimum throughput in each cell. This model is relevant to various applications in communication systems. Finally, we explore potential extensions to our method and its implications. This work is an extension of our previous research on static TDD scheduling.

The analysis focuses on the results of M\"{u}ller et al. published in Phys. Rev. B 93, 144519 (2016), which involves large quantities of vortices. By applying our model, the contribution from the vacancy-induced anomaly is quantified, and it shows that it accounts for a significant Hall anomaly observed in the experiments. Additionally, our analysis supports the earlier finding that the vacancy-induced anomaly is more pronounced in the mixed-state hall resistance measured at higher magnetic fields. Furthermore, our research provides a quantitative estimate of the vacancy concentration in the sample and uses this to examine the parameters that influence the vacancy-induced anomaly, including magnetic field and temperature. Our results suggest that the vacancy concentration remains relatively constant in the range investigated and does not display any significant variation that could be observed experimentally. On the other hand, the ratio of the vacancy-induced anomaly to the normal hall anomaly is found to be sensitive to the concentration of vacancies and shows a notable increase with higher magnetic fields, which is attributed to the greater polarization of the vacancies in this regime. Our theory also predicts that the vacancy-induced anomaly should be asymmetric under the reversal of applied magnetic field, which is confirmed by a quantitative analysis of the data. This finding provides strong evidence for the existence of the vacancy-induced anomaly and the validity of our theoretical model. By examining the behavior of these calculations at and near the critical point, we identify a specific set of scaling relations that can be applied to all correlations and moments exhibiting power-law behavior. As a result, we derive a straightforward yet precise method for determining the exponent that characterizes the divergence or convergence of any given quantity at the critical point. In addition, we show that the scaling of moments follows a regular, fixed-point pattern as one approaches the critical point from either side. This pattern involves a distinctive series of power laws that contain distinct exponent combinations unique to the Ising universality class. We further explore how these power laws give rise to periodic fluctuations in the scaling of moments when plotted against a logarithmic scale. A key feature of this fixed-point behavior is a second-order crossover in the scaling of moments with increasing spacing from the critical point, where multiple power laws become less visible at some intermediate distance. The ever-expanding use of deep neural networks (DNNs) necessitates a constant scrutiny of their reliability in high-stakes applications. Unfortunately, the methods available to evaluate their trustworthiness are limited to broad tests, such as examining their ability to classify 'easy' images, but they fall short in assessing performance on more complex scenarios. A key challenge lies in their inability to recover from a lack of diversity in training data, which can result in them over-relying on extraneous features and being prone to over-fitting. A notable issue arises during their deployment in sensitive contexts, where they may be vulnerable to manipulation through subtle alterations, such as data augmentation. To address these limitations, we propose an innovative multi-agent framework that incorporates a trustworthiness assessment score for each neural network. This score serves as a performance indicator, akin to accuracy, and is utilized to prioritize neural networks that have demonstrated higher trustworthiness for validation sets and new, unseen data. We further integrate an inverse reinforcement learning method to recover from over-reliance on superfluous features and enhance the robustness of our models by promoting them to be more resistant to over-fitting. To counter the risk of over-fitting and artificial fluctuations, we put forward a multi-agent data augmentation strategy, where a subset of neural networks is designated to identify genuine augmentations from fabricated ones. We validated our approach on the CIFAR-100 and SVHN datasets, and the results show notable improvements in the models' performance, with which they successfully avoid the reliance on extraneous features and mitigate the risk of over-fitting. The task of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Despite significant efforts, a major obstacle in resolving WSD incidents is the lack of a comprehensive context-gloss database that could provide a robust understanding of word meanings.  In this paper, we propose an innovative context-gloss enhancement approach for word sense disambiguation.  We utilize a context-gloss dataset to train a word sense embedding model, incorporating both contextual and gloss-based information to inform the embedding.  We leverage the trained model to increase the effectiveness of the context-gloss dataset, refining the word sense embeddings along the way.  Our results indicate that the proposed approach yields a more refined context-gloss dataset, capable of accurately predicting the word sense used in a given context.  Interestingly, we observe a significant enhancement of nearly 20% in the accuracy of the trained model when compared to a baseline approach.  Interestingly, our approach also enables the creation of a robust word sense inventory, showcasing the merits of a context-gloss enhancement strategy over a mere fine-tuning approach.  Our proposed approach achieves the best performance on the SemEval 2007 task 1, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art by a substantial margin of 7.4%.  Furthermore, our approach is effective across diverse word sense distributions.  We anticipate our approach to contribute positively to the development of more effective word sense disambiguation systems.  Additionally, our results indicate potential benefits for the construction of semantic networks and word sense ontologies.  We plan to explore the application of our approach to additional word sense disambiguation tasks in future research. This note presents an analysis for detecting top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions. Top quark production, resulting in $t\bar{t}$ pairs, can be identified through the decay of top and anti-top quarks into $W$ and $b$ quarks. Our analysis focuses on the search for $t\bar{t}$ production at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) running at its highest energy settings, specifically considering 13 TeV proton-proton and proton-lead collisions, as well as 5.02 TeV nucleus-nucleus collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Two scenarios are examined: one for the search for $t\bar{t}$ production in proton-proton collisions with minimum bias triggers, and another for the search in proton-lead and nucleus-nucleus collisions which can distinguish between top quark production and background using global $p_T$ characteristics. Top quark production can be detected in proton-proton collisions at the LHC with 13 TeV and 100 fb^-1 of data, but is less detectable at lower data levels or in proton-lead and nucleus-nucleus collisions. These findings rely on numerical computations utilizing DELPHES, PYTHIA, and FASTSIM. Top quark production can also be discerned through kinematical distributions in proton-proton collisions at higher data levels or in proton-proton collisions with dedicated top quark production triggers. These results provide relevant benchmarks for the further examination of top quark production in proton-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus collisions at the LHC. Additionally, top quark production can serve as a stricture for the LHC to investigate other high-mass processes in proton-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus collisions. Furthermore, top quark production can offer insight into the behavior of high-mass processes in proton-nucleus collisions through comparisons with corresponding cross-sections in nucleus-nucleus collisions, with the added benefit of allowing for the demonstration of the functioning of the LHC detector in heavy-ion mode. This includes the ability to test the detector's system for minimum bias triggers, as well as its system for measuring cross-sections in heavy-ion mode. This study focuses on key elements in text-to-SQL tasks, specifically column names, values, and functions, as well as common SQL commands like insertion, deletion, and update. We aim to expand the scope of database semantic interpretation to address all these elements and commands, even when the input text is unrelated to the SQL code, relying on auxiliary tasks to achieve this goal. We introduce a novel end-to-end model, called CT2SQL, to tackle this challenge. It composes of three components: a column name selection part that selects relevant names from a database catalog based on the input text; a column value prediction part that estimates a suitable value for each column; and an SQL code generation part that combines the selected column names and their corresponding values to create the final SQL code. We utilize a pre-trained language model as the foundation for our model and fine-tune it on a combined database schema and text dataset. We conduct experiments using both a small-scale database and a larger one, and our results show that the CT2SQL model excels in handling complex database semantic interpretation tasks. Additionally, we find that incorporating a column name selection part and a column value prediction part enhances the model's performance on SQL code generation. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyizhang1991/CT2SQL. Furthermore, we have initiated a new challenge for text-to-SQL in Cross-Lingual Database Semantics Interpretation (CL-DBSI) at https://github.com/zhengyizhang1991/CL-DBSI-Challenge and look forward to receiving submissions from interested participants. Our model's performance has also been included as a baseline in our evaluation. We hope this initiative will contribute to the advancement of both text-to-SQL and low-resource language text-to-SQL tasks. It is our hope that this initiative will attract the interest of more researchers in the field. Our paper has been accepted for presentation at the 2022 Conference of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI). Nonetheless, due to constraints related to submission deadlines and paper length at AAAI 2022, some details have been omitted from the paper and included in this updated version. This updated version supersedes the previous one filed for AAAI 2022. Despite the fact that we have initiated a competition associated with this paper and included our model as a baseline, we would like to emphasize that the code submitted to the competition does not reflect the latest updates included in this updated version.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy on networks with privately shared graph information. It covers the application of differential privacy in network settings, focusing on graphs that represent connections and, in some cases, the weights of those connections. These weights can symbolize various values including activity levels, trust, or connection strengths in social networks, the frequency of email or phone exchanges, collaborative efforts, co-authorship, purchasing behaviors, or transaction histories. These graph-based formulations offer vital insights and mathematical representations for a wide range of problems and have significant implications for individuals and communities. However, when dealing with privately shared graph data, several challenges arise, primarily the issue of strata - a concern that is particularly pronounced given the diverse dimensions that such graphs often represent. This paper explores the application of differential privacy in network settings through private learning, specifically highlighting private learning's ability to generate private insights and protect sensitive information when the model is trained on privately shared graph data. Finally, it concludes with the observation that while there are numerous benefits to private learning on network data, the field still lacks a comprehensive framework for private algorithms in this context. This paper suggests a graph-based framework for private learning and highlights the potential of private federated learning on networks. Additionally, it emphasizes the importance of accounting for the graph structure when designing and evaluating private algorithms in network settings. This includes considering the graph's impact on privacy-utility tradeoffs, as well as the challenges and limitations of scaling to large, complex graphs. This paper is an extended version of our previous work presented at the IEEE Secure Communications and Networking Conference (IEEE SACN 2021). It has since undergone significant revisions, including a reorganization of the content, the addition of new sections, and a more comprehensive exploration of private learning on network data. To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating engaging narrative captions to complement them. This paper introduces an innovative approach called MusicCaption, which leverages Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) to generate descriptive texts for playlists. MusicCaption focuses on summarizing the auditory content of music, bypassing the need for visual information from album art. It combines a auditory content feature extractor, comprised of a pre-trained neural network for music embedding generation, paired with a sequential model capable of narrative creation. This paper showcases MusicCaption's capabilities through experimental evaluations, including assessment of its produced captions and comparative tests against human-generated descriptions. The results indicate that automatic captions are not only feasible but also preferred over empty descriptions and certain human-created captions. This has the potential to enable auditory descriptions of dynamic content, such as continuously updated music playlists. Furthermore, this approach may be adaptable to describing other visually inaccessible content. The code for this project is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/shane79/MusicCaption. This new framework is applicable to any observable and is relevant for examining non-equilibrium situations. A specific study using these hydrodynamic equations found agreement with previous findings for a semi-classical, mean-field model, and also uncovered a distinct damped mode in one-dimensional situations, which arises from the interplay of interaction effects and spatial confinement.
