Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. The source code of our method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/DCAN. For activity recognition, our results show a slight decline but still remain competitive with existing methods. Moreover, our method has shown the ability to handle real-world applications with DCAN being applied to YouTube Video Search. The application code has been made available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/DCAN-Search. Additionally, our method has been evaluated on Human Semantic Parsing Dataset (HSP-Dataset) and our method outperforms baseline performance. This paper addresses this shortfall by introducing a standardized testing framework that enables the evaluation and comparison of fuzzer technology. We apply this framework to a renowned dataset containing over 1,000 previously discovered vulnerabilities and test it on a suite of popular binary executables. We make both our methodology and the underlying data publicly available to facilitate the comparison and evaluation of future fuzzer innovations. Additionally, we provide analytical insights into the characteristics of high-quality fuzzers, and we highlight potential areas for improvement in the field. Finally, we make all associated technical data publicly accessible as well. Following the success of pretraining techniques in models like BERT, several methods have incorporated similar strategies into the domain of continual learning. These approaches often involve tying the fine-tuning task to the continual learning setting, thereby implicitly assuming that the continual learning task is representative of the broader problem domain. We challenge this assumption by demonstrating that a straightforward baseline, which freezes the pretraining dataset but allows the model to adapt to changing task datasets, outperforms the current state-of-the-art continual learning models that involve additional pretraining. We based our evaluation on the CoOp dataset, a collection of datasets curated with the intention of continuous release notes on the GitHub CodeOcean blog, consisting of 50 classes that the model is expected to recognize across 2000 anonymized images. The model's performance is assessed on the basis of its accuracy on classifying newly encountered images during the learning process. The code for this project has been made available on CodeOcean at https://codeocean.io/c/0JqXeJ. The model's performance data has been uploaded to the MendeLyo dataset at https://doi.org/10.17604/j9wq437g. Additionally, we introduce the Cont-LinEvalClas metric to evaluate the linearity of a model's classification output, and utilize it to analyze the linearization of our proposed baseline and other continual learning models. The study shows that the proposed baseline achieves comparable performance to the current state-of-the-art models on the evaluation dataset, while exhibiting increased linearity when compared to these models. The improved linearity of the proposed baseline suggests that the non-linear adaptation strategies that involve additional pretraining may not necessarily yield superior performance in the continual learning setting. The code for the Cont-LinEvalClas metric has also been made available on CodeOcean at https://codeocean.io/3T8wvDg. The findings of this study may have implications for the development of continual learning models that involve the freezing of pretraining datasets. The study also demonstrates the linearity of the proposed baseline and the current state-of-the-art models, which highlights the potential for linearization of continual learning models. This final installment concludes our comprehensive study of the global behavior of solutions to the given one-dimensional parabolic equation. The specific equation in question is $u_t = (bu_x + p(u))_x + \sigma(u) + g(x,t)$ with certain given conditions on $b$, $p$, $\sigma$, and $g$. It has been established that when the initial data converge to distinct equilibria, the solution exhibits oscillatory behavior. This theorem is a key outcome of this research and provides a generalization to numerous other equations, including reaction-diffusion and advection-reaction-diffusion equations with rough data. A separate chapter is devoted to a related problem where the goal is to determine a solution to the given equation given additional information about the solution's time-dependent behavior. This problem is solved through the creation of a Hamilton-Jacobi equation with a discontinuous initial condition, which in turn enables the recovery of the solution. This process involves introducing an auxiliary variable that represents the solution's spatial average, which in turn leads to a new equation and, ultimately, a characterization of the solution in terms of its limiting behavior as time increases. We present a new efficient algorithm for computing the maximum probability ordering (MPO) of a binary discrete graphical model, building on previous work by Chan and Darwesh (2020). We demonstrate that MCF ordering has a higher likelihood than the previous state-of-the-art methods, especially on larger datasets, and show the effectiveness of our approach on several machine learning tasks. Allowing for arbitrary relationships between the absorption and the amount of scattered light, our research identified two distinct regimes governed by photon recoil phenomena. The first regime is characterized by weak interactions between atoms, where the scattering pattern follows a 1/$\sqrt{x}$ form, with $x$ representing the ratio of absorption to scattering. The second regime, marked by strong interactions between atoms, exhibits an irregular scattering pattern. When a concentrated suspension of particles is subjected to high rates of deformation, its viscosity suddenly surges, a phenomenon known as shear thickening. This study investigates the scaling of this shear thickening transition through rapid mixing of shear-thickened suspensions with poor solvents, focusing on the critical threshold at which the shear thickening behavior appears. It is discovered that this threshold is directly proportional to the concentration of particles and inversely proportional to the intensity of the mixing, confirming that the shear thickening transition is controlled by the balance between particle collisions during high shear stresses. This finding is validated by repeating the experiment with different types of particles, and the resulting data reveal that the ratio of the threshold to the concentration remains consistent across various suspensions, amounting to roughly 1.5 times the concentration in this particular scenario. This value is interpreted in the context of existing theories and models of shear thickening. Additionally, this research incorporates dynamic light scattering to measure the size of aggregate networks formed during the mixing process, revealing that their scale follows a similar concentration-dependent relationship and exhibits a distinct break at the same threshold as the shear thickening behavior. This implies that the shear thickening transition represents a first-order phase transition in which the size of the aggregates suddenly increases by three to four times their initial size. This discovery has significant implications for understanding how shear thickening must be triggered in order to maintain its stability upon reduction of the shear stress. Furthermore, this study introduces a new term, gamma-star, which represents the critical shear stress required to break down aggregate networks into smaller sizes, and demonstrates that this stress is significantly higher than the shear thickening threshold, suggesting that shear thickening cannot occur unless the concentration of particles is high enough to prevent the breakdown of these aggregates under low shear stresses. Lastly, this research provides a new framework for classifying shear thickening as either 'gradual' or 'abrupt', depending on how quickly the shear stress is increased, and reveals that the behavior of the suspension changes instantly, as evidenced by the aggregate networks, at a shear stress equal to twice the shear rate multiplied by gamma-star. This study offers a comprehensive framework for understanding the physics governing shear thickening and provides a new perspective on the various theories and models proposed to explain this phenomenon. Furthermore, it highlights the significance of studying the shear thickening transition under conditions of high shear stress and suggests a new approach for investigating this phenomenon, which could be applied to other non-equilibrium phase transitions. Our research extends beyond Selloni's findings, offering a more comprehensive velocity-recoil angle correlation and associated spectra for a three-dimensional analysis. Utilizing a numerical approach to describe the scattering events, our research reveals a strong correlation between the incident velocity and recoil angle, which holds true for both elastic and inelastic scattering scenarios. We establish a statistical threshold to identify high-recoil-angle events linked to small mass changes, and our results demonstrate that these events exhibit enhanced velocity-recoil angle distributions and increased maximum energies. Our research provides new criteria for selecting relevant events for future direct detection experiments, particularly those involving low-mass targets like germanium. An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, focusing on the influence of personalisation on their knowledge of search results. 66 participants were recruited and asked to conduct six diverse Google searches from a list of 24, with some users' search history being tailored to align with prevailing public opinions on certain social issues while their search results were not shown to them.  The participants' subsequent search result rankings were significantly lower for four of the six searches, with the average shortfall being around 12%. This difference in search result rankings was at least 20% for half of the participants, indicating that users may misslessly as much as 20% of relevant information due to Web search personalisation. The findings suggest that Web search personalisation has substantial implications for any assessment or evaluation that is based on search results, especially in contexts where access to all search results cannot be guaranteed. The study also provides implications for the design of search studies, the use of Google's search engine, and the reliance on search results in research and practice. The study's limitations and future research directions are also discussed. The experimental data also raise concerns about the validity of previous search studies that are based on Google's search engine, and highlight the importance of replicating and re-examining these studies in light of the findings presented here. The data and materials used in this study have been made publicly available to facilitate replication and re-examination. The issue of Web search personalisation is widespread, affecting any Web search engine that uses cookies to tailor search results to individual users, and the findings presented here are applicable to any such Web search engine. The study's findings and conclusions are also relevant to any assessment or evaluation that is based on Web search, and the study's limitations and future research directions are discussed in the context of these broader applications. This design builds upon existing facilities like muon accelerators, proton drivers, and 10-20 GeV-scale meson factories. With a focus on comprehensive research, a TeV muon collider could tackle numerous fundamental questions in physics, including investigating new physics beyond the Standard Model, reconstructing the universe's early state, and delving into the mysteries of matter-antimatter asymmetry. Furthermore, this collider design offers versatile capabilities, enabling simultaneous research in various areas such as physics related to dark matter, dark energy, and rare processes. Moreover, this document provides an overview of existing and planned facilities, as well as proposed paths for further research and development. This study introduces the concept of CF-approximation spaces, which serves as a foundation for representing geographic areas through point clouds and enables the performance of spatial operations like distance calculations. A key aspect of CF-approximation spaces is their independence from specific geometric representations, such as Voronoi diagrams or Delaunay triangulations. This research demonstrates that any geometric representation of a CF-approximation space can be considered a Delaunay triangulation of the underlying point cloud, which leads to the development of a reachability analysis method for autonomous vehicles traversing complex environments defined by CF-approximation spaces. Furthermore, this research finds that common point set functions, such as mean and median, can be computed using CF-approximation spaces. These findings provide a theoretical basis for using CF-approximation spaces in various applications, including autonomous navigation and machine learning algorithms. Additionally, this research is an expansion of an earlier paper presented at IROS 2019, which introduced the concept of CF-approximation spaces but focused primarily on its connection to autonomous navigation. That earlier work has been built upon here to explore additional point set functions and is further theorized here; however, the discussion on its application to autonomous navigation has been removed and will be addressed in a follow-up study. What is now a generalized theory of CF-approximation spaces is established as the primary contribution of this research. The term "CF" in CF-approximation spaces now stands for any function that can be computed on a point cloud, which is the main innovation of this research over its predecessor. The term "CF" in the earlier paper referred specifically to the mean function, which is a type of point set function. This modification creates a more abstract concept of CF-approximation spaces that can be applied across various point set functions. What is now a theoretical review of CF-approximation spaces under the name of its type, such as mean or median CF-approximation spaces, is offered here as a review of the field. This research on mean or median CF-approximation spaces can be applied across various fields defined by CF-approximation spaces. In particular, this research on mean or median CF-approximation spaces can be applied across machine learning algorithms that are based on point clouds, which is the reason for updating this paper. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more robust estimator was recently proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on adaptive inputs. A novel technique is presented for reducing the query count to near-linear in proportion to the sketch size, thus making the sketch essentially 'waterproof'. A further analysis is conducted to examine how the proposed technique impacts other functions depending on the top elements of vectors. A general framework is also established for evaluating and optimizing the performance of other functions on top-element vectors. A specific application is then explored within this framework, namely a least squares regression problem, which demonstrates the benefits of the new estimator over traditional methods even without consideration of adaptivity. A specific query complexity trade-off is achieved for this particular problem, offering a significant improvement over prior studies by a factor of at least 10 when compared to prior studies on non-adaptive inputs. A further analysis is conducted to examine how a dimensionality reduction technique called JL, which is commonly used in conjunction with CountSketch sketches, may impact the performance of the new estimator, which reveals that it may result in a reduction of near-log factors, which can be overcome by a modified version of the technique, leading to a query complexity trade-off that is within a factor of 5 of the best known results for non-adaptive inputs. This paper addresses the challenge of conducting measurements at a distance from a moving body using single-point laser Doppler velocimetry (SP-LDV). A major restriction of SP-LDV is that it can only detect velocity components perpendicular to the laser beam, and this must be overcome in order to acquire full two-dimensional velocity component information. This goal can be achieved by positioning two SP-LDV systems in line with each other at a distance from each other, and adjusting their laser beams so they are perpendicular to one another. However, this setup poses another difficulty, as it must be precisely maintained during the movement of the body being studied, as any misalignment could result in the contamination of the velocity measurements with an unknown component. This article discusses the development of a method to accurately perform these measurements, and the necessary setup required. A case study is presented, involving the use of this setup to study turbulent flow, and the results obtained from the measurements are validated by comparison with those from a multi-point LDV system. The findings show that the distance between the SP-LDV systems can be up to five times the boundary layer thickness without significantly impacting the results. The developed method has the benefit of making SP-LDV systems more easily transportable and operable in a variety of settings. It is also demonstrated that the method is applicable to bodies with curved surfaces. The article also explores the possibility of adapting this setup for the study of rotating and deforming geometries. The term 'distant operation' is proposed to describe this new approach to SP-LDV, and its potential for use in a wide range of engineering and biomedical applications is identified. The paper is particularly relevant to the study of heart valve and fan blade flows, as these bodies often require the use of a distant operation setup in SP-LDV. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates (PPPs) in enhancing transmission electron microscope (TEM) resolution has been the subject of recent research. These PPPs can dynamically alter their optic function, potentially emulating the performance of an ideal spherical aberration-correcting lens. The present investigation aims to evaluate the potential of PPPs as a corrective measure for spherical aberration in TEM, rather than relying on a custom-made spherical correction lens. The study utilizes a Monte Carlo simulation to assess how PPPs can mitigate the detrimental effects of spherical aberration when imaging non-flat samples, considering various sample tilts and curvature radii. The simulation demonstrates that PPPs can proficiently correct spherical aberration in TEM, surpassing the design's specified Rayleigh criterion in all tested conditions, with an average improvement of one order of magnitude. Conversely, an image quality degradation was observed when attempting to correct for a sample's curvature using its tilt, resulting in a significant decrease of at least two orders of magnitude below the design's specified Rayleigh criterion in all tested conditions. These findings validate the efficacy of PPPs in correcting spherical aberration in TEM, thereby providing a viable alternative to custom-made correction lenses. Moreover, this research raises the possibility of PPPs being adaptable for a wide range of TEM applications, encompassing both flat and non-flat specimens, albeit with the limitation of potential image quality degradation in certain situations involving curved samples. Consequently, this study suggests that TEM practitioners should be cautious when interpreting results obtained with PPPs, particularly when dealing with curved samples, until a comprehensive understanding of this technology is achieved. The potential of PPPs to facilitate simultaneous spherical and chromatic correction in TEM has also been explored, revealing that these devices can effectively mitigate both types of aberrations, thereby enhancing the microscope's overall performance. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the greatest challenge in TEM is likely to be tackling chromatic distortion, which presents a pressing issue that demands urgent attention from the TEM community. The discovery of PPPs has provided a solution to the problem of spherical aberration, albeit unintentionally, and it is now essential to direct the community's focus on finding a solution to the problem of chromatic distortion. The study's findings also highlight the value of theoretical simulations in the development of new concepts and technologies, showcasing the benefits of a collaborative approach between experimental and theoretical electron microscopy groups. The investigation's outcomes also highlight the benefits of open-access publishing, which facilitated the community's swift response and contributed to a more comprehensive exploration of the issue at hand. Speech imitation, a key aspect of speech-related tasks such as speech translation and speech summarization, has not been effectively addressed using current deep learning techniques. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel end-to-end task called masked speech production, where a model generates a partial transcript of an audio clip. In the training phase, we utilize a masking strategy to generate partial transcriptions, enabling the model to incorporate contextual audio information to generate more accurate results. In our experiments, masked speech production outperformed state-of-the-art baselines in evaluation metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE-L. Notably, our approach achieved comparable performance to strong speech translation models when tested on the LIPS dataset, suggesting that masked speech production is a viable alternative to speech translation. In addition, our model's performance scaled favorably to larger datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world applications. We also introduced a context-aware model variant called CA-MSP, which matches the performance of specialized speech translation and summarization models while requiring significantly fewer parameters. CA-MSP's results indicate that it is an attractive solution for multi-task learning in speech-related applications. Our code and models are available for public access at https://github.com/nyu-bb/maskedspeech. In particular, our pre-trained CA-MSP model for English can be found at https://nyu-bb.github.io/maskedspeech/models/CA_MSP_english.tar. We encourage the broader research community to explore this novel task and our approach in the field of speech processing. Moreover, we release the masked speech production subset of the LIPS dataset, which can be accessed at https://nyu-bb.github.io/maskedspeech/data.html. In contrast to speech translation, masked speech production offers several benefits including lower data requirements, reduced label costs, and the ability to learn from unlabeled audio data. However, this task also introduces new challenges such as speech recognition errors and the lack of explicit boundary annotations, which must be addressed by the model. Our approach has the potential to accelerate the development of speech translation models and reduce the costs associated with label acquisition. Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the relationships between black hole spin, mass, and the emission of electromagnetic radiation to determine the characteristics of a specific class of ultralight bosons. By considering a range of boson masses and examining their effects on the electromagnetic emission of quasars, this study identifies a distinct subgroup of quasars with emission consistent with their spin rates being governed by a specific mass range of ultralight bosons. The research finds that the gravitational interaction with these ultralight bosons leads to the depletion of energy from the electromagnetic field surrounding the quasars, a phenomenon that occurs within a mass range of $\log_{10} (m_{\rm oz}/10^{-12}) \simeq 2.5\pm0.5$. 

By taking into consideration the effects of superradiance, i.e., the draining of energy from the electromagnetic field due to the interaction with these ultralight bosons, and accounting for the decline in electromagnetic emission as quasars age, this research is the first to utilize quasars with spin rates derived from their electromagnetic emission patterns. It identifies six quasars with spin rates greater than expected, a trend not observed in control samples. The characteristics of these quasars, with spin rates indicating a specific mass range of ultralight bosons, differ from typical quasars in several aspects: they exhibit greater electromagnetic emission, a different spectral distribution, and a reduced jet spin rate. These quasars with elevated spin rates, all containing black holes with masses greater than $10^9$ M$_{\odot}$, emit electromagnetic radiation due to the superradiance effect, a phenomenon that occurs when the electromagnetic field interacts with the ultralight bosons, a state that cannot be achieved with standard model particles. The findings of this research provide experimental evidence to support the existence of ultralight bosons with non-zero spin and a mass range of $10^{-12}$ eV. The discovery of these ultralight bosons could have far-reaching implications for the development of new experimental searches for dark matter, a phenomenon composed of ultralight bosons, and could potentially explain the existence of magnetic monopoles within quasars. In this study, a quantitative analysis of this process in the zebrafish retina reveals that the distribution of nuclei at both the upper and lower layers conforms to a diffusion model, supported by observations of evenly spaced, migrating nuclei. Furthermore, by applying this diffusion concept to S-phase marked nuclei, it is observed that the retinal progenitor pool is maintained through a balance of nuclear entry and exit rates during interkinetic nuclear migration. These findings suggest a revised understanding of interkinetic nuclear migration as a cellular process driven by forces related to the tissue's state of differentiation and cell cycle progression. The data presented in this study also highlight the complex interplay between these factors that govern the migration of retinal progenitor cell nuclei. In addition, this research provides insight into the dynamic behavior of cell nuclei during this process, revealing a mitotic checkpoint that maintains an even distribution of post-mitotic nuclei and prolongs S-phase in nuclei that are destined for division. These observations imply that the distribution of nuclei at both layers is influenced by their distinct cell cycle states. In order to visualize the dynamics of this process in real-time and in vivo, a novel approach was developed to visualize S-phase marked nuclei. This method enables the simultaneous observation of S-phase marked nuclei and the migration of all other nuclei during interkinetic nuclear migration. In addition, this study demonstrates that the distribution of S-phase marked nuclei can be used as an unbiased indicator of nuclear migration patterns. In conclusion, this study provides a quantitative understanding of the distribution of nuclei at both layers and uncovers the cellular processes that govern interkinetic nuclear migration in the zebrafish retina. In order to validate the novel approach developed for visualizing S-phase marked nuclei, a series of in situ hybridization experiments were conducted on fixed retinas. In addition, a new approach was developed to visualize the distribution of progenitor cell nuclei in the zebrafish retina in vitro. We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory for polar active liquids in the presence of randomly distributed obstacles, in two dimensions and above. Our analysis shows that these active materials can maintain a non-zero density despite the hindrances, and we've determined the precise rate at which the disorder affects their behavior. In fact, we've found that the impact of the obstacles becomes significantly more noticeable as the spatial dimensions increase. Furthermore, our model highlights the essential roles that rotational diffusion and quenched disorder play in the dynamics of these active materials. In the absence of these elements, the symmetry of the system would be lost, resulting in rapid changes in the structure of the bulk material. In contrast, the unique coexistence of density and chiral phases is a direct consequence of the interplay between rotational diffusion and disorder. In the simplest case, our theory is applicable to systems with relatively high obstruction densities, and it suggests the presence of a phase transition in the absence of obstacles, where the rotation of the director becomes highly irregular, ultimately leading to the disruption of the material's long-range order. In the realm of quasi-two-dimensional systems with three spatial dimensions, our analysis predicts a more complex phase diagram, where multiple phase transitions occur as the obstruction density is increased. In this scenario, the relative strengths of the head and tail regions of the polar molecules play a crucial role in determining their behavior. Our model also provides insight into the effects of obstructions on the life cycle of polar mesomers, suggesting that they exhibit a lifetime distribution that is governed by an exponential decay, and the influence of the disorder on their dynamics, resulting in a crossover from an exponential decay to a power law, in accordance with the principles of nonequilibrium phase transitions. Our research demonstrates that the incompressible polar active liquids we've studied exhibit distinct features that are distinguishable from those of compressible active nematic liquids, and our findings are a significant expansion of the previous theoretical frameworks for active nematic liquids in the presence of obstructions, presenting novel nonequilibrium phase transitions that govern the behavior of these active materials. In addition, our research offers a groundbreaking interpretation of the experimental results presented by Giacometti et al., in 2015, in the journal Soft Matter, through the reanalysis of the experimental data, and it provides a new mathematical expression that accurately describes the effects of obstructions on the dynamics of active nematic suspensions, predicting the exact values of the exponents that characterize this phenomenon. Researchers within the same institution often rely on their institutional email as their primary means of communication. To secure these communications, institutions typically implement email security policies, which can take various forms such as blocking external email senders, restricting email content, and enforcing anti-virus protection. Nonetheless, certain email security protocols may inadvertently impede collaborative efforts between academics. To address this concern, our study examines the interconnections between the security policies of academic email services and the structural properties of collaboration networks. Through the analysis of email metadata and network characteristics from multiple academic departments across different institutions, our findings reveal a clear correlation between certain security policies and the prevalence of malicious activities, such as blockage and spam attacks, which can subsequently restrict the scale and efficiency of collaborative initiatives. Moreover, our research proposes a general framework for vulnerability assessment in network security, which can be applied across various network contexts. Ultimately, our study underscores the value of conducting human-centered security vulnerability assessments in academic email networks. To this end, our research is focused on enhancing the security and usability of academic email services through tailored security protocols that balance user experience and system protection. The growth of ID documents has generated significant challenges in processing and analyzing them manually.  One such important ID is the Indonesian ID card, which contains a person's biography and is used widely for identification purposes.  Unfortunately, there are limited resources available for Indonesian ID card information extraction when compared to other popular formats like driver's licenses from the United States.  One potential solution to this challenge is to use a combination of Optical Character Recognition and Natural Language Processing to extract relevant information from the ID card.  In this research paper, we demonstrate the development of an Indonesian ID card information extractor using this approach, which yields a mean average precision score of 0.879 when evaluated using 50 test IDs. Determining the physical characteristics of M-dwarfs is crucial for numerous astrophysical applications, including identifying exoplanets in molecular bond, and valuing M-dwarfs as targets for future stellar surveys. Unfortunately, M-dwarfs' low surface brightness in visible light spectra hinders traditional methods of measuring key properties such as mass, radius, and surface gravity. This paper introduces a new UV spectroscopic sample of non-active M-dwarfs, utilizing high-resolution UV spectra to constrain their atmospheric conditions through abundance of elemental abundances, rather than measuring other properties directly. The analysis focuses on 12 field M-dwarfs, and employs a two-stage approach to model the spectra, first considering global properties and then local sections of the spectrum. The results show good agreement with previous measurements for a limited number of comparison stars, and the new method yields consistent abundance measurements. The analysis also reveals a previously unknown star in the solar neighborhood, and the paper explores the relationship between chemical composition and stellar metal content. The new sample's low-energy spectra will be utilized in a forthcoming study to identify molecules such as OH, MH, and H_2. The data are available through the MANGA database and the paper is the first installment in a series of research papers on this new sample of M-dwarfs. Editors: S. B. W arczak, A. K. Johnson, J. D. The study of infinite words leads to numerous applications in formal verification, 
where model checking and property verification are often limited to predefined patterns.
In contrast, our approach allows any specified property to be converted into a 
form that can be checked against any infinite sequence of characters, expanding the 
scope of property verification beyond predefined patterns. This conversion is possible 
for any property defined using regular expressions and finite automata, and our method 
has been proven efficient, requiring only a linear increase in computational resources 
compared to standard model-checking techniques. Our approach has already been tested 
in a practical scenario, demonstrating its potential for real-world applications. 
Our research also explores potential variations of this conversion, considering 
regular expressions versus finite automata, and we identify areas for further study 
in this field. Our approach is available for download and use with the Spin model checker. 
Our research is an evolution of earlier work on property verification, and we are 
currently exploring its extension to directed paths in graphs. 
Key words: infinite words, property verification, regular expressions, finite automata.

Researchers have analyzed collision data with a total of 3 inverse femtobarns of intensity, and through an amplitude analysis of specific two-body decay events, have discovered a notable fluctuation in amplitude data at around 5.0 GeV, which corresponds to the mass of the $\chi_{c}(3872)$ state in $B^0 \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ decays. Additionally, a mass peak for the $\chi_{c}(3D)$ state was found in $B^0 \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ decays through peak reconstruction, and relevant physical properties, including decay widths and form factor behavior, were determined for this state. A distinct fluctuation was also identified in $B^0_s \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ decays, and the branching fraction of $B^0 \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ decays was precisely measured as (15.8 ± 0.8 ± 1.4 ± 0.2) × 10^-5, with various assumptions considered for the $\chi_{c}(3D}$ state's nature. This result supersedes earlier findings.

A machine learning technique known as reservoir computing generates a simplified model of a complex dynamical system from limited observational data. The recent application of this technique, known as Neural Reservoir Computing, allows for the prediction of a system's behavior based on its past states. Our study shows that by analyzing these predictions, Neural Reservoir Computing can pinpoint hidden combinations of initial conditions that give rise to entirely new, unobserved patterns of behavior. This breakthrough provides a data-driven approach to identifying the intricate, high-dimensional structures that underlie a system's dynamic transitions, even when those structures aren't visibly reflected in the system's overall performance. Using a well-known example, the study demonstrates that this capability can be exploited to discover unexplored pathways to new equilibrium states, and this could potentially be applied to complex systems that are critical to many areas of science and biology.

When data is skewed, measuring the central tendency is not as effective with mean-based methods.  The median absolute deviation (MAD) is an important statistic for assessing variability in such situations. Unfortunately, the classic estimator for MAD is biased, which can be a problem, especially when working with small data sets. Alternatively, we propose a new bias-corrected estimator for MAD, which outperforms the classic estimator across various performance metrics including bias, mean squared error, and confidence interval coverage. Interestingly, we show that the classic estimator behaves better when data is less skewed, but our bias-corrected estimator remains a superior option for skewed data and is also applicable when data is symmetric. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our estimator to the half-space depth, a popular depth measure. As a result, our study provides an invaluable contribution to the field of statistical research. Finally, we offer our bias-corrected estimator for free download on R through an available package. 

In particular, modern statistics often employ depth and depth-based measures of central tendency and scatter, which are robust alternatives to their traditional counterparts, but these come with higher computational costs. Interestingly, when working with large data sets, these issues of bias and cost are less of a concern and are instead focused more on visual representation. Conversely, when working with smaller data sets, visual representation becomes a primary concern, but even so, bias still needs to be addressed. Furthermore, our proposed bias-corrected estimator for MAD retains the same computational efficiency as the unbiased estimator, which is based on the median and half of the squared differences, and significantly outperforms the unbiased estimator in terms of bias, mean squared error, and confidence interval coverage. 

Our study provides a valuable contribution to the field of statistical research, particularly in the area of robust statistics, but the focus on bias in descending order is less applicable when data is symmetric. Notwithstanding this limitation, our proposed bias-corrected estimator for MAD still offers a useful alternative to the unbiased estimator. Additionally, we demonstrate the usefulness and applicability of our proposed bias-corrected estimator to the half-space depth, which is another popular depth measure. 

Finally, we would like to express my gratitude to the collaborators and the university that supported this research, but inevitably had to withhold their identities due to confidentiality agreements. In conclusion, our proposed bias-corrected estimator for MAD provides a superior solution to the long-standing issue of bias in estimating the median absolute deviation.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct features such as face parts, body language, and movement, which can indicate the level of a non-human entity being perceived as non-human. In line with this theory, we designed a novel visual stimulus featuring a human face superimposed on the body of an animal, which we termed the 'non-human face' condition. By utilizing this stimulus in functional magnetic resonance imaging, we aimed to investigate how the animacy organization in the ventral temporal cortex is perceived when a non-human entity with a human face is being viewed. The results show a strong response in areas typically associated with the perception of humans, including posterior superior temporal sulcus, fusiform gyrus, and medial superior temporal area, but interestingly, this response was significantly weaker when compared to the response elicited by a human face. This finding implies that the presence of a human face on a non-human body significantly alters the neural activity in the ventral temporal cortex, causing it to respond as if it is viewing a non-human face rather than a human face. This discovery has important implications for our understanding of how the ventral temporal cortex organizes visual information based on the degree to which a non-human entity is perceived as non-human. It also raises questions about the prevalence of human faces in the environment, which could potentially influence children's development of the animacy organization in the ventral temporal cortex. It has been observed that children's ability to distinguish between human and non-human entities in the ventral temporal cortex is influenced by their ability to recognize human faces, which is a skill that takes time to mature. It has also been found that children as young as three years old are able to accurately identify a non-human face condition as different from both human and non-animate stimuli, which provides evidence for the existence of a distinct face-sensitive sub-region in the fusiform gyrus in early childhood. However, the strength of the neural response to this condition continues to evolve throughout childhood, which is unique to the ventral temporal cortex. This evolution is thought to be driven by changes in the brain's visual processing systems as they adapt to the prevalence of human faces in the environment, which is a key factor in the development of the animacy organization in the ventral temporal cortex. The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a calculable pace, supported by the broader conclusion that Dirichlet L-function zeros exert a force pushing zeros from all other automorphic L-functions off the s=1 axis. This finding is backed by two key components. Firstly, it's been established that the Riemann zeta function $\zeta(s)$ exhibits nontrivial zeros with a significant distribution similarity to those of an individual L-function. Secondly, the nontrivial nature of zeros from all other automorphic L-functions can be guaranteed by the application of sieve methods to eliminate potential zeros with a lesser distribution pattern. We examine the relationship between young low-mass stellar cluster formation and
the properties of nearby spiral galaxies. Using IRAC/GLAIR photometry from the S4G
sample of 176 spiral galaxies, we calculate the number of young stellar clusters
in the central regions of these galaxies. Our analysis indicates that the number
of these clusters is linked to the global star formation rate within the galaxy.
In particular, we discovered a strong correlation between the cluster density and
the galaxy's specific star formation rate. Additionally, we found that clusters
in more massive galaxies tend to have larger radii, which could be attributed to a
greater presence of globular clusters acting as gravitational triggers for the
dispersal of cluster members. Our research also reveals that ultra-faint dwarf
galaxies, like Fornax and Sculptor, exhibit a lower cluster density compared to
more massive dwarf galaxies like Leo I and Sagittarius.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-enhanced approach called multiple-round self-evaluation, which allows models to generalize across tasks.
In this framework, we gather a diverse set of samples by drawing from their own internal predictions, then use these examples to refine the model's performance.
We implement this idea through a self-evaluation dataset that's continuously updated over multiple iterations, with each round consisting of filtering a large dataset of internal predictions to remove the most confident examples, thereby creating a diverse and representative dataset that's free from overfitting.
We apply this framework to multiple text-related classification tasks, with results showing significant improvements over current models and even matching their performance in some cases.
Furthermore, we discover that the models developed through this framework exhibit excellent performance when compared to others, even when tested on completely new tasks. 
This approach is particularly useful for large language models like T0 and FLAN as it enables them to generalize effectively to new tasks without the need for explicit fine-tuning. 
We believe this study to be a groundbreaking breakthrough in the field of few-shot learning and cross-task generalization, with immense potential for future exploration and discovery. 
We invite the community to explore this study and our data, with all code and experiments being openly available for reproducibility purposes. 
In conclusion, we successfully demonstrated the capability to develop models with robust cross-task generalization ability and are excited to see the applications and results that the community will yield in the future.

One significant issue in robotics learning from natural language feedback is the limited amount of information provided in each lesson. Typically, an action is either affirmed as correct or deemed faulty and in need of revision. In this study, a key challenge arises from the fact that these labels don't describe the actual underlying state of the world but rather the teacher's perception of the situation. In other words, the teacher's judgment isn't a direct reflection of the actual state but rather an estimation based on their observation of the action's outcome. In this research, a key assumption is that the teacher has a clear idea of what a correct action would achieve in an ideal setting. With this assumption in mind, a crucial finding emerges - if the action is completely disapproved of, it implies that the action made sense in the real world but didn't align with the teacher's standards. On the other hand, if the action is partially accepted, it indicates that the action didn't make sense in the real world but managed to meet the teacher's expectations. In essence, disapproval indicates a mismatch between the real and ideal worlds, while partial approval indicates a mismatch in the ideal world. In practical terms, a negative score can be viewed as a penalty for an action that was sensible but didn't align with the teacher's expectations, while a positive score can be seen as an additional reward for an action that wasn't sensible but managed to align with the teacher's standards. In this study, a key insight is that the teacher's judgment forms a partial order over possible actions - in effect creating a way to prioritize actions. In this research, several key concepts are introduced, including the idea of a teacher-student symmetry, the formulation of a weak consistency condition, and the development of a meta-algorithm that leverages feedback to learn from weak supervision and correct past mistakes. In this study, these concepts are demonstrated through a series of experiments using a simulated robotics environment, and the performance of the proposed meta-algorithm is compared to several baseline methods. In this comparison, the results show that the proposed meta-algorithm is highly effective at learning from natural language feedback in a robotics setting. When imagining hypothetical rain in a given image, we're essentially creating two components: rain and the altered image. Yet, current methods fall short of accurately capturing these elements, resulting in unrealistic rain and compromised image quality. To address this, we develop a disentangled approach that learns to remove rain from an image and then generates new rain to combine with the image, yielding a more realistic outcome. Our method involves a disentangled rain generation process, splitting the process into two steps: first, removing rain from an image by discarding the learned rain features, and second, creating new rain using the extracted features. This disentangled process is challenging to execute directly, so we instead employ a disentangled conditional GAN to achieve this rain-and-image combination. Our proposed approach outperforms the competition in both quantitative and qualitative assessments, and our code is available for public access.

Excessive drug consumption poses a threat to youth, and understanding the underlying factors is crucial for developing and executing effective prevention plans. This study aims to evaluate the risk of drug consumption among adolescents through the lens of the Five Factor Model of personality. Our research delves into the nature of the quark-gluon plasma using deep inelastic scattering as a lens, drawing from quantum chromodynamics. We've derived the structure function of the quark-gluon plasma within the framework of quantum chromodynamics, specifically within the soft and medium-modified hard scattering limits. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that the Bjorken limit of finite quark mass corrections, gluon distribution modifications due to medium interactions, and virtual photon splittings into $e\gamma, eG, eq\bar{q}$ systems, are all encapsulated within the structure function. Additionally, we've explored DIS effective temperature, $T_{\rm DIS}$, as a function of energy and coherence length, finding it relevant for describing intermediate-scale phenomena within the medium. Moreover, we've established the relationship between $T_{\rm DIS}$ and the point of instantaneous interaction within the medium, often denoted as $\sim 1/\omega \sim 1/\omega_\perp$. We've also investigated the transverse momentum broadening of vector mesons within the medium, demonstrating that it results in an additional width of $\sqrt{\lambda/4\pi}T\omega_\perp$, with implications for the interpretation of experimental data from deep inelastic scattering and heavy quarkonia production. Ultimately, our research underscores the significance of considering medium modifications to photon splitting processes and virtual photons scattering off quarks and gluons, which hold the key to deeper understanding of the quark-gluon plasma through deep inelastic scattering. Their sequential design leads to implications regarding their capacity to
understand and process syntactic properties, specifically those involving
concord – the agreement between words within a sentence.
As neural networks are typically trained on the basis of distributed
representations, it is crucial to analyze whether their performance on tasks
that require concord is achieved by recognizing the syntactic structure or
the semantic content of the words.
We examine this question by creating and testing a series of sentence
classification models on the Basque language, given that Basque is highly
inflected and has complex concord patterns.
The results show that neural network models perform below average on tasks
that require concord, and analysis of their errors reveals that they often
confuse the grammatical gender of Basque nouns.
Furthermore, when we introduce a word that indicates the semantic content
of the sentence, the performance of the neural network models drops, implying
that they are processing the words based on their distributional properties
and not their inherent meaning.

syntactic analysis and the study of linguistic phenomena in general. As the

We develop a variational approximation, based on the piecewise-rigid map model, for structured solids undergoing large deformations and breaking events. This approximation utilizes the phase-field method to define a non-convex and stationary functional that represents the energy expended by the solid during its deformation and fracture process. By establishing the existence and uniqueness of the solutions, we demonstrate that the approximated energy functional, as the phase-field parameter decreases, converges to the original piecewise-rigid map functional. Furthermore, we derive a compactness result for sequences of functions satisfying certain bounds derived from the piecewise-rigid map functional. This result enables the recovery of the exact solution after a finite number of re-assembly operations for any given boundary value problem. Ultimately, we provide a computational algorithm to solve the approximated equation and subsequently obtain an estimate of the original solution. This algorithm is verified using numerical experiments and images. Additionally, we apply this approximation technique to light transmission measurement data to reconstruct 2D maps of fracture energy in concrete using a computational model with spatial variability. This reconstruction enables accurate simulation of additional light transmission measurements near the same concrete sample. This technique may also be adapted for use with other piecewise-rigid map applications. We examine leptoquark compositeness by investigating Drell-Yan production of lepton-quark pairs, considering all possible lepton and quark generations, within a third-generation gauge vector leptoquark model. To accurately assess this process, we perform next-to-leading order calculations for the relevant parton distributions and combine them with precise parton shower simulations to assess the Drell-Yan production of leptoquark-composite vector bosons. To facilitate this investigation, we developed the OneLoopLibrary, an open-source mathematical framework for evaluating complex loop integrals and fundamental processes at next-to-leading order. As a primary demonstration of its capabilities, we present the explicit results for this Drell-Yan production in the form of grid files, suitable for use in conjunction with the pythia8 event generator through the OneLoopLibrary's interface with pythia8. Furthermore, we anticipate that this library will contribute significantly to the interpretation of existing and future particle collider data within vector leptoquark models. In particular, we highlight its potential to bridge the gap between theoretical predictions and experimental comparisons with data, incorporating detailed theoretical simulations of complex processes and interactions within the context of the standard model and its extensions. In addition to this particular demonstration, the OneLoopLibrary has already been used to interpret results from the Large Hadron Collider and is being utilized in ongoing analyses at the ATLAS and CMS experiments, as well as in discussions with the particle physics community. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained tasks like point reaching or grasping, imitation learning applies to complex tasks involving nonlinear constraints and avoiding static or dynamic obstacles from unknown starting points. However, these challenges increase the degree of difficulty by an order of two, as imitation learning usually assumes that the starting position and task target are known in advance. In such cases, additional constraints are often addressed by penalizing the cost function, yet this method fails to account for important aspects like kinematic constraints and potential field costs. This paper introduces a generalised imitation learning framework called EKMP that leverages multiple experts to account for linear and nonlinear constraints from unknown starting points at the task target. The framework also considers non-linear hard constraints and obstacle avoidance along the learned trajectory. This is achieved through a optimized routing technique that considers various experts, their respective costs and constraints, to be combined with the maximum variability principle to select the most suitable expert at each knot point. The resulting algorithm is tested on a seven degree-of-freedom industrial robot arm learning to pick up objects from unknown positions on a table, replicate a circular motion and navigate through a maze in three-dimensional space. The experiments show that the EKMP algorithm is highly efficient, producing a cost that is up to 50% lower than the baseline method and is successful in all the pick-up trials it was challenged with. The breakup of Africa and South America was thought to have occurred as a result of the separation of the Atlantic and South Atlantic rifts.  However, studies suggest that Africa and South America were already separated by as much as 3,000 to 2,500 million years before the Atlantic rifts formed.  Additionally, evidence indicates that South America drifted north for about 1,000 million years before it connected with Africa, which further changes the early history of the Atlantic rifts.  The early separation of Africa and South America resulted in distinct continental plates, often referred to as Congo and South America plates, which eventually merged.  These separated continents maintained their individual mantle roots under went distinct geophysical and geochemical processes, causing them to behave as separate convective cells.  The merged Congo and South America plates then moved apart over South America, resulting in extension and thinning of the continental crust across western Brazil, Paraguay and parts of Argentina, often referred to as the Western Brazil Craton.  This process occurred from about 200 to 100 million years ago during the final stages of the South Atlantic rifting.  The Eastern Brazil Craton maintained its individual mantle root and distinct geochemical and geophysical processes, and as such, did not experience the same extension and thinning as Western Brazil, Paraguay and Argentina.  The Eastern Brazil Craton behaved as its own convective cell, until it connected with the Western Brazil Craton, and together they formed the Brazilian plate.  The break-up of the South American supercontinent occurred from about 180 million years ago during the Jurassic to the Cretaceous period, and the resulting Atlantic and South Atlantic rifts formed over South America, and later over Africa, and eventually separated the continents of Africa and South America. A proven strategy in unsupervised segmentation is information maximization, which can be achieved through mutual information maximization or contrastive learning. This approach leverages unannotated images to extract meaningful representations from given images. However, a challenge arises when applying these methods, as they often rely on overcomplete codes, which can lead to fragmented or distorted boundaries when transferring the learned representations back to the original images. This limitation is particularly problematic in medical image segmentation due to the intricate boundary information commonly found in medical images. To overcome this boundary loss issue, a new framework is proposed that incorporates a segmentation branch into the code regression process, allowing the codes to accurately capture boundary information. Additionally, a code regularization technique is suggested to prevent overfitting, and this proposed framework is compared to a state-of-the-art self-supervised segmentation framework. The results of the comparison show that the proposed framework outperforms the baseline in most cases, and the method is robust as evidenced by a confusion matrix showing few instances of poor performance. Furthermore, a further analysis is conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework on different models. Human-made and machine-generated texts exhibit distinct writing styles, which are reflected in the words they use. While similar words with the same meaning, also known as synonyms, are predictable in human language, our analysis reveals a more complex pattern in machine language, with a greater diversity of synonyms used. To better understand and measure this phenomenon, we developed a wordpair-based approach to compare human and machine language. Our analysis of a wordpair network with 329k pairs identified 11 key differences between human and machine language. For instance, machine language favors more diverse synonyms, which can lead to less precise semantic representations. Reasoning about "what if" scenarios, whether expressed in individual statements or as part of a narrative, is a fundamental ability essential for effective decision-making. This ability is critically tested when considering counterfactual situations that explore outcomes stemming from distinct scenarios. As a case in point, counterfactual thinking plays a significant role in the field of law, particularly in the context of "but-for" causality, which asks "what would have happened if not for this particular event?" In this paper, we introduce the Discrete Situation Counterfactual Ontology (DISCO) framework to formalize complex "what if" statements that describe change within a specific context over time. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of a machine learning-based approach in generating plausible situation descriptions and evaluating the correctness of counterfactual situations. This evaluation shows that human assessors consider certain generated situations as at least somewhat plausible. We also showcase a web-based interactive application that allows human users to explore the workings of the DISCO framework. This framework holds promise for enhancing the capabilities of current language models by enabling them to engage in counterfactual reasoning about real-world situations. As an example of this potential, we show improvements in descriptive outputs generated with the aid of DISCO, as judged by human evaluators, when compared to the baseline of current large language models. These improvements indicate a potential for further enhancements in the coherence of generated texts. We further expand the scope of DISCO to encompass continuous situations by introducing the C-DISCO framework, which allows for the expression of counterfactuals in regards to continuous contexts. We employ a set of situation descriptions derived from descriptions of physical systems and demonstrate the effectiveness of both DISCO and C-DISCO frameworks in generating coherent situation descriptions with the aid of large language models. This is exemplified through generated descriptions of both discrete and continuous situations, which are evaluated by human assessors and found to be at least somewhat plausible in many cases. We make available our code, data, and applications on an open-source basis at: https://github.com/CompLAb-UW/disco-situ. This work is a part of the broader CompLAb-UW project, which can be found at: https://complab.org/. Both of these resources provide cutting-edge cutting knowledge for both continuous and discrete situations. Additionally, we introduce the Situ counterfactual data set, comprising over 10,000 situation descriptions and counterfactual situations obtained from online articles, which can be accessed at: https://github.com/CompLAb-UW

Our analysis classifies the disks into three magnetic domination regimes: low-strength, intermediate-strength, and high-strength. These groups exhibit distinct characteristics in relation to stock market trends and patterns, and our analysis reveals notable instances, including the historical separation of large-cap and small-cap assets, and more recent divisions based on technological and sustainable focuses. Our research also explores practical applications of this model in identifying underperforming assets and potential market inefficiencies. The rapid growth of mobile healthcare is generating substantial interest in developing secure and private healthcare systems.  Despite the benefits, the risk of sensitive medical information being compromised discourages users from fully utilizing these systems.  To address this concern, a novel approach is required to protect user privacy while facilitating effective model updates.  This paper presents FedHealth, a pioneering framework for federated learning that enables the seamless transfer of knowledge between institutions, promoting a data-driven approach to healthcare through wearable devices.  FedHealth's distinctive feature is its dataless and labelless design, enabling a model to be trained on a device without accessing sensitive healthcare data or assigning labels, while also facilitating batch updates on a server.  This innovative design results in FedHealth having a minimal communication overhead, making it particularly suitable for devices with limited bandwidth.  The FedHealth framework is particularly adaptable to scenarios involving multiple institutions, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through a comprehensive evaluation of a cardiovascular disease diagnosis model on real-world datasets.  The encouraging outcomes of this evaluation highlight the FedHealth's potential to become a leading framework in the field of healthcare through wearable devices.  The framework's code is available for repurification and further development at https://github.com/seyedmahmoud/FedHealth. This pioneering approach paves the way for the development of secure, privacy-preserving, and data-driven healthcare systems via wearable devices. This study explores a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states are divided into distinct groups and vary over time, with some groups being more expensive to navigate than others. Our goal is to minimize the total cost by switching between these groups, with the restriction that the time spent in each group is measured at a micro-level. To tackle this issue, we first establish the existence of an optimal strategy by reducing the complexity of the problem through multiple adjustments, including scaling down large differences in costs, introducing a common base cost, and normalizing the costs to fit within a limited range. Finally, we address the situation in which the costs exhibit discontinuous fluctuations and maintain the efficacy of our approach by normalizing the costs. This research is an extension of a previous study conducted by Fornasier and Mallozzi in 2019. Additionally, we present an explicit formula for an optimal strategy in a simplified version of the problem, where the costs of transitioning between states are piecewise constant and vary over time, with some groups being more expensive to navigate than others. Temporal sequence analysis is a complex task with numerous applications, including the analysis of life science measurements such as gene expression, protein levels, and metabolic network activity. Despite the wealth of expression data available, many experiments involve only a single time point due to the high cost and complexity of simultaneous multi-time point measurements. This paper introduces an innovative strategy to guide the learning of temporal sequences using prior knowledge. Our model leverages this information to predict unseen time points, even with very short sequences. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through the analysis of life science measurement data, including expression profiles and metabolic network activity. Our results show that guided learning outperforms traditional methods, especially with short sequences. This technique holds significant potential for life science research, as it can be integrated with collaborative learning methods to analyze even higher-dimensional temporal sequences. Our work lays the foundation for the development of advanced models that can accurately predict multiple temporal sequences related to the same entity, such as distinct gene expression profiles. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found in diverse settings like newspapers, websites, and technical documents. While they facilitate compact communication, they also introduce difficulties in comprehension, as they often lack clear connection to their corresponding phrases. In order to tackle these challenges, a comprehensive approach is required, involving both automatic acronym detection and disambiguation strategies. In response to the absence of a unified, user-friendly platform for exploring and assessing existing approaches as well as developing new ones, we present MadDog. This web-based application allows researchers and users to test existing models, submit their own datasets, and evaluate the performance of various machine learning algorithms against the application's internally generated benchmarks. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. This study deviates from the point-based approach, instead focusing on topological nodal lines – one-dimensional structures that separate the momentum space into distinct areas with different topological properties. The authors outline the theoretical framework for quantifying a nodal line's topological characteristics and review recent experiments that demonstrate nodal lines in photonic, phononic, mechanical, and electrical systems, showcasing their versatile realization across diverse artificial materials. These experiments not only contribute to the theoretical understanding of topological nodal lines but also propose new concepts for creating robust photonic and other non-electronic analogs of zero-mode states and other topological phenomena. Furthermore, the authors discuss the distinctive features that are essential for maintaining a non-trivial topological phase in nodal lines and the potential for replicating complex topological phenomena in natural and man-made systems through artificial lines and surfaces. These ideas are expected to extend the scope of topological physics beyond electronic systems and may find applications in optimizing the performance of optical devices, mechanical systems, and other non-electronic phenomena. Finally, the authors highlight the promise of combining theoretical descriptions and experimental techniques to design and replicate topological phenomena in diverse systems and suggest exploring topological physics in the context of quantum simulation, inspired by the principles of topological protection. This study is expected to catalyze further research into the intricate relationships between topology and symmetry in condensed matter physics and quantum mechanics. In the course of this review, the authors' own research conducted at the University of Oxford has been referenced. Due to the rapid advancements in this field, this review is intended to provide a general overview rather than a comprehensive analysis of the topic. This note presents a new, more delicate version of the b-principle, focusing on orientable maps requiring a highly inflexible way to point. As proof, we show that a family of oriented maps can be successfully pointed if and only if a specific flexible pointing is achievable, with this equivalence being the core content of the modified b-principle. Additionally, we utilize this result to demonstrate the validity of a modified version of the Mumford Conjecture, concerning the geometric properties of smooth surfaces with negative curvature. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the b-principle and the classical 1.5-dimensional bordism problem, an problem of geometric topology. Finally, we present an informal discussion on the limitations and potential extensions of the modified b-principle. With respect to the Mumford Conjecture, we previously proved that a certain family of surfaces with negative curvature does not contain essential surfaces of high genus. Persuasive promotional videos are becoming increasingly influential in shaping consumer behavior and promoting social causes through various mediums such as e-commerce platforms and non-profit initiatives. Leveraging artificial intelligence, these engaging videos can be automatically created to target specific goals, addressing the challenge of mass customization in video content. This field, known as persuasive video generation, encompasses a broad range of applications, including marketing, politics, and non-profit endeavors. A comprehensive examination of the state of the art in PVG is complex due to the diverse nature of its sub-domains, such as entertainment, education, and biomedicine, as well as the varying types of persuasive content, such as commercials and, for example, videos promoting healthy behaviors. This survey paper focuses on two primary aspects of PVG: (1) the development of artificial intelligence models capable of creating entertaining and engaging content, such as movies and games, and (2) the creation of more substantive, informative content aimed at educating viewers about particular topics. Additionally, this survey explores issues related to the design of persuasive video content in an automated fashion, including the challenges of achieving goal-based targeting and ensuring the generated content's quality and consistency. Finally, this survey concludes with an exploration of the role of data, the development of more effective algorithms, and the creation of specialized platforms for creating persuasive videos automatically. These considerations include issues related to the collection and utilization of data, the creation of more sophisticated artificial intelligence models, and the development of customized infrastructure for generating such content efficiently. As the field of PVG continues to evolve, it is essential to address fundamental questions regarding the ethical implications of creating automated persuasive content, the potential biases in data-driven approaches, and the impact on viewers, particularly in areas such as biomedicine and education, where the audience may be more vulnerable. These ethical considerations pose significant concerns and highlight the need for more research in this domain. This survey paper is intended to serve as a comprehensive reference for researchers, providing a thorough examination of the state of the art in PVG, while also highlighting the complexities, challenges, and pressing concerns facing this field. This survey paper is also designed to serve as a reference for practitioners, offering a detailed exploration of the various techniques and methods employed in PVG, while also highlighting the numerous applications and use cases for creating automated persuasive video content. This survey paper is the first of its kind to provide an in-depth examination of the field of PVG, encompassing both entertaining and informative content, as well as a comprehensive overview of the various techniques and methods employed in this domain
