This paper examines the effect of court-ordered therapy on mental health among individuals within the criminal justice system. Leveraging a law change in California requiring convicted individuals with a mental health diagnosis to participate in a therapy program, we studied how this policy influenced their mental health outcomes. The analysis compares the changes in symptom severity among those required to attend therapy to those who were not affected by the law change and therefore did not have to participate in the program. Employing difference-in-differences and propensity score matching methods, we discovered that participating in the therapy program led to a notable reduction in mental health symptom severity. Additionally, we discovered that this benefit extended to family members who were also affected by the individual's mental health, as their reports of the individual's symptom severity also decreased. The analysis further revealed that the therapy program's benefit in reducing mental health symptom severity was more pronounced for certain types of mental health conditions. A widespread issue in medical image segmentation, especially under semi-supervised conditions, is over-reliance on training data, leading to a failure to generalize well. To mitigate this, many methods integrate regularization terms into their optimization frameworks. We take a fundamentally different approach, questioning the necessity of complex models and sophisticated optimization methods. We argue that the issue of over-reliance arises from model drift, and therefore, simply returning to the original model parameters after training would rectify the problem. With this in mind, we propose a remarkably simple semi-supervised medical image segmentation framework, wherein we add a regularization term directly linked to the difference between the model's training and frozen parameters. This results in the incorporation of unused supervisory signals from unlabelled data, without introducing new optimization variables or conflicting objectives. Notably, our method converges to a consistent solution and generalizes well to unseen data, as evidenced by state-of-the-art performance in multiple benchmark datasets, including MIO1, ACDC, DD5K and Hep2D. Code is available at https://github.com/zhengyangwang/CRSS.

Understanding complex dynamics in quantum many-body systems is a major challenge in studying statistical mechanics and quantum dynamics. Recent advances in machine learning and numerical methods have paved the way for graph neural networks to successfully capture key properties of these complex systems. We've developed an open-source framework based on graph neural networks that can efficiently track local properties of quantum many-body systems in discrete spacetime configurations. This framework allows for the precise interpretation of its predictions through a hidden state representation, providing valuable insights into the underlying system's dynamics. We've applied our framework to a notable example, the XXZ quantum spin chain, demonstrating its ability to make measurements about entanglement, correlation lengths, and other key properties with little computational expense. Our results show that graph neural networks can effectively emulate the behavior of quantum systems, even in the presence of chaos, and we've observed that they can distinguish between chaotic and ordered phases of the model. Our framework is a significant step towards using machine learning tools to study the intricate dynamics of quantum many-body systems. We've made the technical details of our method and the associated data accessible on an open-source repository, available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.07967. We believe that this type of machine learning approach has vast potential for being adapted to other use cases and we're eager to see it evolve further. We've also explored the concept of extending graph neural networks to open quantum systems, and we've begun exploring the possibilities of using this type of machine learning approach to study the interplay between quantum systems and their environment. We've initially explored this idea using the example of the quantum spin chain in interaction with a motionless bath, described by a Lindblad master equation, and we've examined the possibility of describing the evolution of the system's entanglement using graph neural networks. This paper presents an original work on generalized maximum likelihood estimation (GMLE), a new method for averaging parameters in mixtures. We demonstrate that GMLE outperforms existing methods, including maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and the Charnock estimator, which we improve upon. Additionally, we explore potential applications of GMLE to broaden the scope of structural estimation in economics, particularly in contexts where sampling involves a mixture design, inclusion exclusion principles, and sampling from a mixture of independent populations. We also examine the theoretical properties of our enhanced estimator and provide simulations to further evaluate its performance. We are open to feedback and collaborations on this research.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks have generated node embeddings that preserve structural and semantic information from the input graphs. To validate the effectiveness of these embeddings, a more controlled evaluation setting is required. One such approach involves assessing whether the generated embeddings correctly capture the proximity relationships between nodes, as defined in the original graph. In this paper, a new dataset, Twitch Players, is introduced for the task of evaluating graph neural network node embeddings in a proximity-preservation context. Twitch Players is derived from the Twitch player subgraph, where each node represents a player with 64 distinct feature attributes. Two types of edges connect players who are close in rank after completing a multiplayer Twitch game, inducing a highly connected graph with many cycles. The evaluation of this dataset shows that existing GNNs, when tested on Twitch Players, are able to preserve the original graph structure but often fail to maintain the predefined proximity relationships. As a result, Twitch Players provides a robust challenge for the development of novel graph neural network architectures that prioritize proximity preservation. The dataset's unique characteristics also make it an ideal candidate for evaluating the applications of graph neural networks in multi-class classification settings. The evaluation of Twitch Players against multiple graph neural network architectures has resulted in a new dataset that raises important questions and demonstrates the effectiveness of both a proposed architecture and a role-guided node embedding method. The complete Twitch Players dataset, along with the code for the paper, is publicly available at: https://github.com/aleksandar-eric/Twitch-Players. The paper has been successfully peer-reviewed and accepted for publication in the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2023. Additionally, a short video accompanying the paper can be found at: https://www.aleksandar-eric.com/twitch-players. Word count: 320.

Membrane rafts are semi-firm areas within cell membranes composed of various lipids and proteins. They have been linked to numerous cellular functions, including the organization of biological signaling, the transmission of mechanical forces, and the distribution of membrane components. The concept of rafts originated from their perceived firmness and ability to move freely within the cell membrane; however, recent studies have raised doubts about their existence due to apparent discrepancies in their supposed firmness and mobility. This review aims to examine current understanding of membrane physics in relation to raft theory and proposes a more nuanced view of membrane dynamics, emphasizing the role of temporary gaps within membrane fluids as raft equivalents. It suggests that these gaps, resulting from combinations of lipids and proteins interacting through various forces, can provide a more flexible and adaptable means for the cell to organize its membrane components. It is essential to consider not just the structural composition, but also the dynamic nature of these entities, which we propose to name 'gastro's in honor of their origin, the cell's gastrointestinal system. This review also discusses recent studies on membrane dynamics, raft structure, and the proposed gastro model, offering a theoretical framework that could be applied across different cell types and potentially used as a basis for the development of biomimetic membranes. It concludes by exploring potential applications of the gastro model in understanding biological processes and its potential as a blueprint for artificial membranes with self-organizing properties. Furthermore, it proposes future research directions for the gastro model, including studies on gastros using advanced imaging and simulation techniques, as well as the investigation of gastros in model and living cells using X-ray fluorescence, and the development of artificial membranes based on the gastro model. It is clear that the concept of free-moving, firm membrane rafts no longer holds merit; instead, it is time to embrace a more nuanced view of the cell membrane, with a focus on temporary gaps and their role in the self-organization of membrane components. It is essential to revise our understanding of the membrane raft theory and consider a new paradigm that incorporates a fluid membrane with transient pores, as this will allow for a deeper comprehension of the cell's internal functions and provide a solid foundation for the development of innovative artificial membranes with self-organizing properties. Galactic mergers significantly shape galaxy evolution, especially those occurring at $z\le 1$. This study examines how magnetic fields affect major galaxy mergers at $z\le 1$, considering various possible influences. We use high-resolution, multi-scale simulations to model the effects on gas and stellar discs during mergers, accounting for magnetic field amplification through the development of instabilities and shear layers. Our results show that a strong magnetic field can impede the disruption of gas discs by tidal forces, causing more gas to conserve its original rotational pattern and increasing the likelihood of circumnuclear starbursts. Additionally, we find that a strong magnetic field can stiffen both gas and stellar discs, leading to more direct superposition during mergers and higher probabilities of disc mergers. Our findings are relevant to observational studies of galaxy mergers and provide insights into the magnetic field's impact on galaxy evolution and structure. This research lays the groundwork for further investigations into the effects of magnetic fields on galaxy mergers, especially in relation to the formation of magnetic fields in starbursts and the development of galactic dynamo. This introduction focuses on these issues, and our follow-up study will delve into the influence of magnetic fields on galaxy merger products. Rounding is an essential concept used in modeling real-world phenomena, including the estimation of uncertain quantities. However, standard extreme value theory methods assume that measurements follow a specific distribution after being rounded to the nearest integer. In contrast, we develop a new statistical approach that accounts for the effects of rounding on the collection of discrete data, including negative biases resulting from underreporting. By leveraging rounded values, we obtain new insights that can inform the analysis of such data. In particular, we show that the sum of rounded counts follows a discrete distribution that takes into consideration the rounding process, which we refer to as the SAR distribution. We also establish connections between the SAR distribution and traditional discrete distributions, and we explore ways to estimate model parameters using rounded data. Our results are illustrated through an analysis of newly collected data related to guessing one's own age, a classic example of rounded responses. In this context, we highlight potential biases in previous analyses and demonstrate the advantages of our new approach. We make our data and computational tools openly available for reproducibility purposes. These methods and the associated theory can also be applied to other counting tasks, such as the collection of rounded data from fully anonymous participants. In addition, we provide general advice on designing and evaluating estimation procedures on rounded data. These ideas are relevant to any scenario involving the collection of rounded data, including demographic surveys, where understanding quantities such as age, income, or political affiliation is crucial. In such settings, our results offer a foundation for developing and assessing statistical methods that account for the effects of rounding on data collection. In recognition of the pervasive nature of rounding in data collection, we propose the term "ambiguity" to describe the range of possible values associated with each data point, encompassing any deviation from the true value due to the rounding process. We define corresponding notions of ambiguity for dependent variables and establish results on the distribution of aggregated data under ambiguity. These findings provide a theoretical framework for statistical modeling that takes rounding into consideration and offer practical guidance for estimating model parameters using real-world data. In the context of our age data, we investigate the effects of different rounding processes and associated ambiguity profiles. This occurs when the temperature is brought below the N\'{e}el temperature set at 2.12 K. A kind of symmetry known as the $ab$-plane four-fold rotational symmetry holds a significant influence over the magnetic characteristics in this region. In an in-depth investigation, we found that the two main energy scales which govern the magnetic behavior, namely the exchange interaction and the on-site energy, are closely matched, resulting in an extremely precise balance that is easily disrupted by any crystallographic disorder, ultimately leading to the preservation of the magnetic wavevector $\mathbf{q}=\left(\frac{2}{3}, 0\right)$ that corresponds to the minimum energy state. Infrared spectroscopy also provided us with the opportunity to look for any signs of magnetic excitations within the infrared range, and the absence of same was confirmed through small signal detections in certain regions. On the other hand, the spin wave excitations share a more intricate origin, and their resonant behavior at very low energies is a result of a kind of flat mode that forms within the two-dimensional structure, and it may be possible to observe this phenomenon in better signal-to-noise ratios through the use of higher-intensity neutron beams. These unique properties, along with the presence of half-magnetization per atom, make the study of spin wave excitations in GdInO$_3$ particularly engaging from a theoretical standpoint. Furthermore, the unique characteristics of the exchange interaction in this compound may also be susceptible to modulation by an electric field, which could potentially result in the creation of a quasi-two-dimensional electronic analog of a skyrmion, a topologically non-trivial magnetic structure, through the application of an electric field to the sufficient degree. The task of allocating a set of indivisible items among a group of self-interested players, who make rational decisions in order to maximize their own gains, is an important problem in the study of mechanism design and economics. This challenge becomes particularly complex when the number of players exceeds the number of items available, as it then becomes impossible to guarantee a fair allocation to all players. This paper addresses this problem by investigating whether indivisible goods can be fairly distributed among a group of strategic players of any number, as we establish the existence of fair strong truthfulness under pure Nash equilibria for any number of players and a specific allocation method known as Round-Robin. Additionally, we examine the efficiency of these equilibria and find that, under certain conditions, they can be arbitrarily far from optimal. This research is further expanded to consider the concept of envy-free allocations, and we identify certain combinations of players and items for which Round-Robin allocations are inherently envy-free. The methods we develop are also adaptable to a variant of combinatorial auctions known as XOR-auctions, and we demonstrate the fairness of Round-Robin in this setting as well. This paper presents an original model that assesses tail risk using a unique threshold estimation method, integrated into a robust GARCH framework. The proposed framework, called RTA-GARCH, utilizes a non-linear autoregressive component and a unique self-renewing threshold process to estimate the size of tail events. The study shows that the RTA-GARCH model outperforms competing models, including the EGARCH and CJS-GARCH models, in forecasting Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall. Specifically, the results indicate that the RTA-GARCH model generates more accurate forecasts than the alternative models, both in terms of the mean and the median, for a wide range of financial assets across different market conditions. Furthermore, the RTA-GARCH model demonstrates superior performance compared to the hidden Markov model and the regime-switching GARCH model. The findings support the idea that the RTA-GARCH model can provide more accurate forecasts of tail risks than traditional GARCH models. Removing a line from a smooth cubic threefold in projective four-dimensional space yields a hyper surface of dimension three, which we term a "banner variety." When a rational curve intersects this banner variety in a specific manner, a corresponding point is identified on a related dual variety. A connection between these points exists, forming a relation that can be expressed through the use of quantum $K$-correlators. This paper introduces an expansion of quantum $K$-correlators that is relevant to banner varieties, demonstrating that their coefficients match the positions of certain points on the dual variety. Additionally, we establish that these coefficients follow a pattern defined by a motivic version of a universal function first introduced by M. Henniabat and N. Manohar. This universal function appears as a factor in the expansion of another mathematical construct, known as the Fock-Goncharov block. As such, the properties of the universal function can be inferred from the properties of the block, and vice versa. Both the universal function and the block exhibit a combinatorial aspect tied to the structure of a specific type of graph, which we term a "triple". This relationship between the universal function, the block, and these graphs provides insight into the underlying nature of quantum $K$-correlators. Furthermore, the paper includes a discussion on the properties of the graph triples, namely that they are minimally non-decomposable, and that any component of a decomposed triple will retain its initial name, albeit with the prefix changed from "triple" to "double" or "single". A natural extension of these graph triples will also be explained, involving the addition of extra edges, which we term "quadruples". These quadruples will likely play a role in further expansions of quantum $K$-correlators, specifically those involving a self-intersection number of an irrational curve that is twice the number of lines the curve intersects. While these data sets are often vast, containing thousands or even millions of information-rich items, their inaccuracies can prove devastating to the performance of the machine learning model. The field of data debugging is focused on identifying and mitigating these errors to enhance the reliability of machine learning models. Unlike traditional approaches that concentrate on individual components of a machine learning pipeline, such as classification models or data preprocessing methods, this work is dedicated to debugging the entire pipeline. Our primary objective is to determine the portion of the model's performance that is attributable to the data sets it uses, rather than its architecture or other factors. Our analysis of 24 clusters yields statistics on radio sources containing millisecond pulsars, low-mass X-ray binaries, and other non-pulsar radio sources. Additionally, calculations of radio source densities around the MAVERIC clusters and elsewhere in the Galaxy are performed. The results show that the total density of radio sources containing low-mass X-ray binaries and millisecond pulsars in the Galaxy is significantly higher than the observed density within the MAVERIC cluster sample. This task can be viewed as a completion problem, where the goal is to infer a set of large-sized hyperedges from limited node and edge information. Current methods primarily rely on traditional graph-based models and pairwise interactions, which are insufficient to capture the more comprehensive relationships present in hypergraphs. In contrast, our proposed Hypergraph Completion Network (HCG) model leverages a guided hypergraph reconstruction approach, integrating both local and global signal information to recover a rich hypergraph structure. The model is mathematically defined using a flexible hypergraph adjacency function that can accommodate various types of relationships, and is optimized using a biologically-inspired hypergraph optimization module. Our comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our HCG model over baseline methods. Notably, we observe significant improvements on a biological data set containing cellular protein-protein interactions. In our accompanying analysis, we explore the characteristics of this dataset and provide a thorough evaluation of our proposed HCG model. Furthermore, we investigate the performance of HCG on datasets with distinct graph structures and evaluate the model's scalability in relation to hypergraph size. Lastly, we explore the interpretability of our model through the identification of crucial hyperedges and provide a qualitative analysis of its predictions. In conclusion, our work offers a pioneering solution to the guided hypergraph reconstruction problem and provides a comprehensive exploration of our approach through extensive experiments and a detailed analysis of a newly introduced benchmark dataset. In offline multi-agent reinforcement learning, effective learning is possible without exploration, relying solely on previously collected data. A key challenge here is dealing with an excessive number of possible collaborations or 'paths' between agents, which can hinder identification of the optimal policies. This problem is particularly pronounced in complex environments with many agents. One promising approach to address this issue is to prioritize learning from 'good paths', which are estimated by the performance of the resulting policies. By leveraging a novel 'good path' measure and an associated ranking mechanism, we develop an efficient framework to learn from just the top-performing collaborations. This framework is theoretically sound and is experimentally proven to be highly effective, especially in scenarios with multiple agents in complex environments. Our findings suggest that learning from the best collaborations can be quite selective, often focusing on just a small percentage of the most effective teamwork. This is particularly evident in scenarios with single agents or in relatively simple multi-agent settings, where the best performances can sometimes account for over 90% of the overall performance. Our work is significant because it is the first to explore the potential of offline multi-agent reinforcement learning from just the most effective collaborations. This research is relevant to applications such as video game AI, where the evaluation of AI agents is often performed on their performance in previously played levels. Our results indicate that, with this approach, the evaluation of AI agents can be significantly more efficient, focusing on just the most challenging levels. This is particularly evident in scenarios with single agents or in relatively simple multi-agent settings, where the best performances can sometimes account for over 90% of the overall performance. Our work is an extension of prior research on offline reinforcement learning, which focused on individual agents, and is an initial exploration of the potential of offline multi-agent reinforcement learning. This research is ongoing, and future work will investigate further the challenges associated with offline multi-agent reinforcement learning. In particular, future work will focus on developing a more rigorous analysis of the proposed method and on exploring alternative approaches to offline multi-agent reinforcement learning. In addition, future work will investigate the application of offline multi-agent reinforcement learning to more complex scenarios, such as scenarios with multiple groups of collaborating agents, and will investigate the use of natural language processing techniques to enable the evaluation of AI agents based on the performance of their names. This research is ongoing, and future work will focus on the following open issues: developing a more rigorous analysis of the proposed method, exploring alternative approaches to offline multi-agent reinforcement learning, and investigating the application of offline multi-agent reinforcement learning to more complex scenarios.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and generating both gamma-ray and soft X-ray emissions. In quantum computing, performing the same task with fewer qubits is always more desirable. This study compares various applications of two qubits and multiple qubits in the toric code, focusing on error correction. We examine two scenarios: one where two-qubit operations are the only allowed interactions, and another where any multi-qubit interactions are permitted. To analyze this, we selected several two-qubit gates, including the CNOT, SWAP, Frederich, and Bell gates, and investigated their capabilities within the toric code framework. Our investigation reveals that none of these two-qubit gates can perform a multi-qubit operation like the Fredkin gate when restricted to two-qubit interactions in the toric code. However, the CNOT, SWAP, and Bell gates can achieve any two-qubit operation when allowed multi-qubit interactions are considered, and interestingly, the swap gate can also accomplish a multi-qubit permutation task. Furthermore, we found an explicit transformation for deriving a multi-qubit operation from its two-qubit counterpart within the toric code. This general finding is not limited to the toric code, as it applies to any stabilizer code that can protect one qubit against individual errors. Consequently, any two-qubit operation can be converted into a multi-qubit operation in such a scenario. Additionally, we discovered that the swap gate enables a multi-qubit permutation task when multi-qubit interactions are allowed, and this result is applicable to codes that can protect more than one qubit against individual errors. Furthermore, we explored several multi-qubit operations in the toric code, including a certain permutation task, and found corresponding transformations for obtaining any two-qubit operation from a two-qubit gate like the CNOT gate when multi-qubit interactions are allowed, leading to the conclusion that such a two-qubit gate can perform a multi-qubit operation like the Fredkin gate in this context. Lastly, we consider the implications of this research for quantum simulation, as it highlights the significance of controlling qubits one at a time when simulating the behavior of qubits under different operations within a quantum error-correction code. This study further reveals that swap-gate-enabled simulations allow for the transfer of a specific type of correlation between qubits, and this might be useful in circumventing constraints imposed by quantum simulation parity-check constraints. This knowledge could be beneficial in designing more effective quantum algorithms for simulating the behavior of qubits within a quantum error-correction code. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then selects the most relevant component and communicates its index to the mobile terminal. During downlink transmission, the mobile terminal estimates the GMM and determines the closest component, allowing efficient information exchange via index feedback. Simulation results demonstrate that this approach outperforms traditional methods in terms of performance-diversity gain tradeoffs and yields improved spectral efficiency. Furthermore, an analysis of complexity and decoding difficulties in 5G systems is presented, revealing opportunities for optimization in future standards. The proposed scheme's performance in 5G systems is evaluated, showing a significant performance gain over reference designs, especially in high-frequency scenarios. The proposed algorithm's performance relies heavily on the accuracy of GMM training, which is ensured by incorporating a quality control measure. For over five decades, researchers have been aware of an intriguing link between supermassive black holes and the cosmic microwave background. This connection was initially seen in the gas content around galaxies, and more recently in the host galaxies themselves. A key factor in this relationship is likely tied to the rate at which stars form, a process influenced by the Bondi accretion rate and mass loss of the associated black holes. Using data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, a study of Bondi accretion rates across 341 galaxies has revealed a limit on the rate at which they can lose mass. The findings suggest that when the mass of a galaxy's central black hole exceeds 10 million solar masses, the Bondi accretion rate cannot exceed a certain threshold in galaxies that possess a certain type of spiral structure. The established boundary is crucial in explaining the universal, non-linear star formation laws observed in galaxies. Additionally, it implies a limit on the rate at which black holes can grow through accretion, and suggests that the maximum growth rate of these black holes occurs when the Bondi accretion rate reaches a critical value, where the rate of mass loss in the host galaxy is maximized. As a result, the discovered constraint provides new insight into the relationship between galaxies, their central black holes, and the cosmic microwave background, and may help to explain the broad class of low-luminosity active galactic nuclei featuring a thin accretion disk. Furthermore, the study sheds light on the growth patterns of massive black holes during the early and late stages of galaxy evolution. The research also reveals an intriguing link between the detection rates of these active galaxies and the structure of galaxies that host them, and an equally intriguing connection between the rate at which stars form in galaxies and the detection rates of certain active galaxies, where the latter occur when the Bondi accretion rate exceeds a certain threshold in galaxies that possess a certain type of spiral structure. The study also uses data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory to investigate the detection rates of low-luminosity active galactic nuclei targets, and discovers a significant increase in the detection rate of these targets when the Bondi accretion rate exceeds a certain threshold in galaxies that possess a certain type of spiral structure. The study offers a new model for predicting the detection rate of active galaxies at a given luminosity, and provides new insights into the relationship between galaxies, their central black holes, and the cosmic microwave background. We examine the formation of binary millisecond pulsars in nuclear star clusters of massive galaxy hosts. Using a semi-analytical model for the structure of these star clusters, we find that they form compact binary systems containing a neutron star or black hole through three-body encounters and gravitational instability. The creation rate of such systems is influenced by the cluster's mass and galactic environment. A higher cluster density leads to a greater creation rate of binary systems, while the rate is slowed in clusters with low density. The detection of such binary systems by the Advanced Laser Interferometer Observatory is also predicted, with a possible detection rate of 0.4 to 40 detections per year, dependent on the sensitivity of the detector and specific characteristics of the binary systems. This detection rate is expected to be influenced by the presence of star clusters in the galaxy's central region. Furthermore, the detection of these binary systems may provide insight into the early universe, with a possible detection rate of binary systems formed during the universe's early stages, with a specific detection rate of 0 to 13 per year, dependent on the characteristics of the universe during this period.

This article explores the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-like spaces, specifically on BMOA*p and its analogue BMOQ*p. BMOA*p is a part of the family of BMO-type spaces, defined as the image of moduli of continuity through the Fourier coefficients. Our focus lies in identifying the maximal subspace of BMOA*p that supports a semigroup of composition operators under certain mappings f_n. We establish that this maximal subspace is f_0 in BMOA* and demonstrate its equivalence to the maximal subspace of BMOQ* when the moduli of continuity are replaced by the quasiconformity moduli. Furthermore, we investigate the maximal subspace of BMOQ*p with respect to the integral operator T_\alpha, proving that it is the image of \alpha through the Fourier coefficients. This conclusion holds for both continuous and quasiconformal operators, providing a comprehensive exploration of the maximal subspace of BMOA*p with respect to the integral operator T_1, the identity operator. Additionally, we highlight the connection between the composition operators and the integral operators, as well as their combination, offering a main result for the continuous case. This research is also applicable to the Volterra integral operator, a special case of T_1. We demonstrate that the maximal subspace of BMOA* with respect to the Volterra integral operator is the image of the real part function through the Fourier coefficients. This finding is a key outcome of our exploration. Finally, we examine the maximal subspace of BMOQ* with respect to the composition operators and the integral operators, establishing a connection between them, and providing a main result for the quasiconformal case. This article is a continuation of our previous work on BMOA-like spaces and semigroups of composition operators, as well as integral operators, as presented in [1]. Humanity has continually sought balanced growth in all aspects of life, and this concept is reflected in the idea of the golden ratio, a perceived ideal ratio of 3:2. The golden ratio has been discovered in nature, art, and finance, often associated with aesthetic appeal and sound decision-making. In the realm of scientific advancement, researchers aim to identify a similar ratio between the production of high-quality knowledge and the overall amount of existing knowledge. To achieve this, a new metric is introduced, based on the structure of citation networks, which can pinpoint optimal thresholds for evaluating scientific progress. Using the citation networks of three prominent scientific journals, PLOS ONE, Nature, and Science, a potential golden ratio of 1.61 was found, indicating that a 61% increase in published papers results in a 39% greater likelihood of a paper being cited more than expected. Furthermore, a model incorporating this ratio can accurately predict the likelihood of a paper being cited excessively, based on the number of authors involved. Additionally, a golden ratio of 1.26 was found for the relationship between the number of authors and the probability of a paper being cited more than expected, suggesting that papers with 26% more authors than the optimal amount are more likely to be cited abnormally. In contrast to previous methods for evaluating citation networks, which are based on arbitrary thresholds, the introduced metric provides a data-driven approach, enabling the discovery of a universal pattern applicable across multiple citation networks. This research demonstrates that a gold standard, often perceived as an ideal but unattainable goal, can be found and utilized in the complex context of citation networks. The study's findings on the golden ratio of citation networks and scientific productivity may be of interest to scholars of science policy, complexity science, and network science. In addition, the introduced metric can be employed to explore other golden ratios governing the behavior of citation networks. In conclusion, humanity's pursuit of balance is reflected in the ideal ratio of 3:2, which has been discovered in nature, art, and finance, and now, in the context of citation networks and scientific productivity. In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: generating safe, data-based predictions for the positions and movements of human drivers. We initially develop a theoretical framework for reliable prediction, given that human drivers adhere to standard rules. To account for uncertainties, we incorporate confidence estimates into our predictions. Building on this foundation, we create a predictive control algorithm that considers not just future traffic light changes but also the predictions of human drivers' behavior. We test our approach with real data and demonstrate its effectiveness. Human drivers generally respond positively to the displays of our algorithm's recommendations. We also conduct numerical analyses to evaluate how various traffic light settings impact our algorithm's performance. Notably, our study shows that certain light settings may lead to decreased following of our recommendations by human drivers. Finally, we investigate the interplay between traffic light timing and the accuracy of our predictions, finding that certain settings may decrease our confidence in predictions. Overall, our study provides a practical framework for managing the safety of connected automated vehicles in urban intersections. To facilitate further development, we make our algorithm and data available for use. 

Further, we investigate two variants of our algorithm, one with basic confidence estimation and a more advanced version utilizing a machine learning model. Our research indicates that both approaches yield comparable outcomes in terms of prediction performance. However, the more complex algorithm exhibits greater variability in results. We also examine the effects of varying traffic light timings on our algorithm, observing that certain settings lead some human drivers to disregard our recommendations more frequently. To better understand human behavior around our algorithm, we conduct additional analyses, and the methodologies employed are suitable for assessing the performance of similar connected automated vehicle systems. 

The code utilized in this research is designed for the evaluation of connected automated vehicle systems at urban intersections and is available for public use at https://github.com/argoshen/PCACAV. The dataset employed in this study, comprising real-world traffic data with annotated bounding boxes, is also accessible for public use at https://github.com/argoshen/PCACAV/tree/main/data. The study's results, including the qualitative and quantitative outcomes, the human subject experiment data, and the comparative analysis between the baseline and machine learning-based confidence estimation approach can be found in the project's GitHub repository. The study's findings provide valuable insights into the development of connected automated vehicle systems for real-world urban traffic applications. To facilitate further development, the code and dataset employed in this study are available for public use.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 10,000 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a staggering increase in simulation processing speed of roughly 100 times, reaching a rate of over one million actions per second on a single CPU core. This improvement, achieved through a combination of low-level code optimizations and efficient memory management, enables researchers to conduct more extensive and varied evaluations of virtual agents in a realistic text-based game environment. TextWorldExpress is made available as an open-source platform for testing the full range of virtual agents in a fast and reliable text-based game. It can be accessed at https://github.com/google-text-to-arrays/TextWorldExpress. This new text-based game challenges virtual agents to interact with complex texts and solve complex problems in a timely manner, further establishing the importance of thorough testing before applying these agents to real-world scenarios. One of the games we present, called the "Biological Reading Game", represents a significant breakthrough in testing the ability of virtual agents to extract accurate information from texts. It demonstrates the feasibility of evaluating the performance of these agents against a measure of speed, representing the number of relevant pieces of information they can retrieve within a set time limit. This evaluation metric, called "inference rate", may be useful in assessing the overall performance of virtual agents in a wide range of applications. It is possible to convert TextWorldExpress into a fully synchronous game program capable of supporting the development of advanced virtual agents using asynchronous techniques. This is shown to result in a significant improvement in the performance of one widely used virtual agent, achieving an increase of roughly 10 times on a single CPU core. TextWorldExpress can also be executed across multiple CPU cores, enabling it to support the development of a wide range of virtual agents. It is possible to train virtual agents using texts that contain a mix of factual and fictional information, such as science fiction stories. It has been discovered that the performance of virtual agents can vary depending on the type of text being used, with some agents excelling in texts that contain action-packed scenes but struggling with quieter scenes, highlighting the importance of thoroughly testing these agents in a variety of settings. Deep learning models like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in sequence classification tasks but are complicated, requiring massive computational resources. This paper presents an LSTM-based algorithm and a custom hardware design for real-time video identification. On one hand, a compressed LSTM model is proposed using the Hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition algorithm, resulting in significantly reduced computational requirements without significantly impairing performance. In simulation experiments, our decompressed LSTM achieved comparable accuracy to the original model on the CMU Multimodal Ensemble dataset. On the other hand, a custom hardware design featuring interconnected memory blocks is described, enabling efficient, in-line computation of decomposed data. Built into an Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC), this design demonstrated unprecedented energy efficiency and low latency in real-time video identification. Compared to a generic System-on-Chip (SoC), our ASIC-based implementation outperformed it in energy, with a  13.6x energy reduction and 2.7x lower latency. As practical applications for this design are limited due to large model size, a further optimally compressed model is proposed, achieving near-real-time performance while maintaining only slightly lower identification efficiency. This optimized model enables highly efficient video identification in real-time. In contrast to other deep learning models like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), LSTM's input and output gates enable stable gradient descent, facilitating tensor decomposition. Although this complexity also increases model size, this property enables the decompressed model to accurately identify sequences with high stability. Furthermore, this custom hardware design is suitable for any compressed RNN-like model employing self-connected memory blocks, offering a generally applicable solution for deep learning algorithms with temporal classification capabilities. This research provides a novel solution for the widespread challenge of deep learning-based sequence classification under computational and energy constraints. As such, it is expected to significantly impact the development of efficient deep learning models in various applications and across multiple domains. In addition, this work is expected to facilitate the design of more effective compressed deep learning models that are capable of being seamlessly integrated with custom hardware. This integration is critical in fully leveraging the performance capabilities of modern computing hardware, such as Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) and ASICs. Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the large-data setting, thanks to the effective utilization of data augmentation and transfer learning.  However, many NLP tasks across the world are constrained by limited data, slow generation, and high labeling costs, necessitating the development of cost-effective methods that can efficiently leverage small, high-quality training datasets.  This study scrutinizes the effectiveness of data augmentation in such scenarios, examining 11 datasets, 8 NLP tasks, and exploring the impacts of augmentations, scheduling, and domain shifts.  Our findings reveal that scheduled data augmentation, combined with careful selection of augmentations, can significantly improve performance when compared to a baseline model, with an average improvement of 6.5% across all settings.  Interestingly, we observe that scheduled data augmentation exhibits reduced performance degradation when compared to a baseline model, achieving a 10% improvement in the average absolute reduction in performance in challenging domain adaptation scenarios.  Our research is ongoing, and we plan to continually update the study with additional insights and experiments.  The current study, along with all experiments and models, is publicly accessible for replication and reference at https://github.com/PranavPrabhu/NLP-Limited-Dataset-Aug.  We invite fellow researchers to collaborate and build upon this empirical study.  Key findings and observations from this study will be presented at the EMNLP 2022 conference.  As the field of NLP continues to evolve, it is essential to address the limitations of data availability, labeling costs, and generation time, and our study represents a crucial step in this endeavor, with implications for both theory and practice.  Furthermore, it paves the way for exploring novel methods that can efficiently leverage small, high-quality training datasets, and we believe it is essential for the community to prioritize empirical research in this domain. Ridesharing and other auxiliary transportation services are altering the dynamics of traditional taxi industries worldwide. To stay competitive, some cities have implemented regulations requiring taxi drivers to invest in these alternative transportation networks. However, the effectiveness of these policies depends on several factors, including the level of investment required and the level of freedom given to taxi drivers in choosing between transportation networks.

Research on transportation network markets has identified key factors such as cost, income, and taste that influence drivers' and riders' decisions. However, the interplay between these factors and the level of investment required for auxiliary transportation services is not well understood. To address this knowledge gap, a model of transportation network markets has been developed, allowing researchers to analyze the impact of investment requirements on the profitability of taxi medallions.

The model has several interesting properties, including but not limited to: it reaches a socially optimal equilibrium under certain conditions; the impact of investment requirements on medallion prices depends on the level of freedom given to taxi drivers; and restricting cross-sided payments can either increase or decrease the value of medallions.

The study of a laboratory market has confirmed the predictions made by the model, revealing that the level of freedom given to taxi drivers plays a critical role in determining the value of medallions. Furthermore, an extension of the model has been developed to examine the impact of introducing new transportation networks on the value of medallions, and the results of the laboratory study support this extended model. The research has contributed to the design of an auction mechanism that considers the interplay between transportation networks and has implications for policy design in the taxi medallion market. The model has potential applications in designing auctions for other industries with network effects. The model has also been applied to study the value of taxi medallions in New York City. The data and the design of the experiment are publicly available. The study has been ongoing since 2019 and the latest laboratory data collection ended in 2022. The formation of this hexagon is attributed to a periodic rotation of strong wind patterns rather than being a stable geometric shape. The mechanism driving the metal-insulator transition in oxide materials has long been a subject of investigation.  Recent studies suggest that this phenomenon may be influenced by surface modifications, especially for materials like V$_2$O$_3$, which exhibit significant reactivity.  To further understand this, we conducted a comprehensive examination of the surface composition and structure of V$_2$O$_3$ ultrathin films using photoemission spectroscopy, low energy electron diffraction, and scanning tunneling microscopy.  Our analysis revealed that in vacuum, the surface of V$_2$O$_3$ ultrathins exhibits VO surface oxygen atoms that bond with the underlying V atoms, forming bridging oxygen sites.  However, when exposed to oxygen, these VO sites transform into VO$_2$ patches, and when exposed to water or formic acid, they become covered with hydroxyl or formate groups.  Our findings suggest that these surface modifications significantly impact the electronic structure and cause the metal-insulator transition, which is evident from resistivity, spin-polarized photoemission, and scanning tunneling spectroscopy analyses.  Our study demonstrates the critical role surface modifications play in determining the electronic properties of reactive materials like V$_2$O$_3$ and highlights the need for controlling the environment during material synthesis.  It also presents an opportunity to design functional materials with desired surface properties and explore the functionalization of materials using various molecules. Conversely, this limit is shown to be avoidable when error detection gate operations are perfect, a finding that is universally true for any quantum error correcting circuit. Our research also reveals distinct boundary patterns for specific quantum computing architectures, such as square lattices and random graphs, which may guide the design of future quantum computing hardware.

To date, conventional machine learning techniques used in text analysis have largely overlooked these elements. This paper presents a novel approach to classify discourse indicators, including both explicit and implicit forms, which are utilized extensively in discourse theories like RST and DDIA. These indicators serve multiple purposes such as signaling contrast, causality, and temporal relationships between sentences. To this end, we've developed DiscSense, a dataset that encompasses 31 different discourse functions, encompassing 9 categories like contradiction and causality, and covers both explicit and implicit indicators. This dataset comprises 25,000 annotated instances from comprehensively selected discourse bases, including RST-DT, DDIA-DT, and Universal Discourse Tree Bank. Interestingly, our findings indicate that models excel at classifying explicit indicators but struggle with their implicit counterparts. To overcome this challenge, we've proposed an enhanced model named Multi-Scale Deep Learning Model, which achieves remarkable improvement in accuracy. This model's effectiveness is further substantiated by a practical application, where it enhances the performance of sequence-to-sequence models on discourse-aware machine translation. Our model and DiscSense dataset are now available for public access. This study's findings are relevant to the development of swimming robots that can operate effectively in various fluids, such as ocean waters.

We introduce five rigorous methods for assessing the reliability of these predictions and establish a comprehensive benchmark to evaluate and compare them. This benchmark encompasses diverse datasets, ranging from astronomical images to medical diagnoses, as well as diverse tasks, including classification, construction of density functions, and function approximation. We are confident that our framework and benchmark will be instrumental in advancing the field of uncertainty quantification in neural networks, enabling them to be more trustworthy and more versatile in their applications. These experiments demonstrate the benefits of the proposed framework, and the results of the experiments are presented in the form of illustrations and detailed discussions. However, creating these higher-order Weyl materials in a pure form is extremely challenging due to unavoidable linear Berry phases causing their degeneracies to shift, thus masking the hallmark of a higher-order Weyl material. Recently, researchers have proposed two possible solutions to circumvent this issue: using natural materials with multiple Weyl points to cancel out linear Berry phases or developing a new theoretical framework to focus on the square-root of a higher-order Weyl tensor. In this study, we introduce the concept of square-root higher-order Weyl materials, which can be realized through linearized dispersion relations resembling those of natural three-dimensional Weyl semimetals. By applying a linearized expansion to the square-root higher-order Weyl Hamiltonian, we derive the precise linearized dispersion relations and Chern number combinations, which are invariant under spatial and temporal transformations and thus maintain their integrity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the square-root higher-order Weyl Hamiltonian can be achieved through a simple lattice model, providing a feasible pathway for experimental realization using ultracold atoms or lattice fermions. This study explores how anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by a weaker equatorial bulk rotation speed relative to the polar regions, affects the stability of solar-type dynamos and predicts possible magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars. We based our simulations on global three-dimensional mean-field simulations using the "template-domain" approach, representing a slowly rotating solar-type star by accounting for the rotation-induced generation and transport of magnetic fields. In contrast to sun-like differential rotation, anti-solar rotation causes the generation of toroidal magnetic fields via the $\alpha$-effect to be suppressed at the equator and enhanced at the poles. As a result, magnetic flux accumulates at the poles and is ejected via magnetic winds, while the equatorial regions experience reduced magnetic flux expulsion. This altered magnetic field distribution leads to increased toroidal shear and subcritical instability at the poles, resulting in magnetic field reversal and cyclic behaviour. In stars with rotation rates below 0.5 times the present solar rotation rate, the generation of magnetic toroids is dominated by shear instability rather than the $\alpha$-effect, leading to magnetic field reversal at both the equator and the poles and possible bi-modal solutions. This work suggests that stars with rotation rates below this threshold may exhibit magnetic cycles and multiple poloidal fields. Furthermore, we find that increasing the star's convective efficiency reduces the stability requirement for rotation, while enhanced internal heat sources or heat loss decrease the stability requirement, and both increased convective flux blocking and stratification decrease the stability requirement, leading to possible bi-modal solutions in more stable setups. This research provides a theoretical framework for understanding possible magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars and the distinctive light curves and activity patterns they produce. Additionally, it highlights the significance of rotation in stars with masses one to three times the mass of the Sun. In conclusion, global three-dimensional simulations offer a promising approach for studying the internal magnetic field generation and the associated starlight variations, and this study lays the groundwork for examining other dynamic processes in stars with magnetic fields. Finally, considering the vast population of slowly rotating magnetic stars with possible cycles, their study holds great potential for furthering our understanding of magnetic cycles in stars. This research also raises the question of whether stars with masses one to three times the mass of the Sun, which exhibit cycle-like behavior in their light curves, are actually experiencing magnetic cycles induced by their internal dynamo. This study formulates curved K-theory spectra within the framework of motivic homotopy theory and establishes key properties. Specifically, it demonstrates that curved simplicial presheaf functors lifting the motivic K-theory spectrum exist and are unique up to rationalization. Furthermore, it shows that these functors can be represented by motives with respect to rationalization, and it identifies the motivic cohomology sheaves of twisted generalized motivic cohomology theories within the category of simplicial presheaves. Additionally, it proves that the motivic cohomology sheaves of twisted generalized motivic cohomology theories are represented by geometric motives with respect to rationalization. Finally, it establishes connections between curved K-theory and twisted generalized motivic cohomology theories. These findings build upon earlier work by Kahn-Levine where the homotopy theory of motivic simplical presheaves was employed, and they involve collaborations with Kahn, Levine, Hoyos Murrieta, Jannsen, Sato, and Yamaki. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model and analyze these events. However, estimating the parameters of this model is complicated due to the need to compute the excess rate and conditional intensity functions, especially when the past data is extensive. In addition, many existing methods for parameter estimation rely on approximations and can result in inaccurate confidence intervals. To address these challenges, we developed a new Bayesian approach for fitting and assessing the nonlinear Hawkes process model. Our method uses a random walk Metropolis-Augmented Data Augmentation (MW-ADA) algorithm to efficiently sample the unobservable excess rates and estimate the model parameters. We also derived the moments of the estimated conditional intensity and excess rate functions. Our results demonstrate that our Bayesian approach outperforms existing methods in terms of bias and variability. We applied this method to various datasets, including datasets of natural disasters, online messages, and neuronal activity. Our study sheds light on the performance of our method and the properties of the estimated functions. Furthermore, a Python package called Kins, which is based on our method, can be used for the flexible estimation of multi-type point processes. Kins is capable of handling a wide range of nonlinear functions, including Gaussian, edge-stable, and neuronal network functions. It also includes innovative visualization tools to display the estimated intensity and excess rate functions. We invite researchers to collaborate with us on further development of this method. We have made the source code of our study as well as Kins available on GitHub. On top of that, we have set up an online repository for sharing and analyzing multi-type point process data called Porecopedia. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of laser-plasma optics a pressing issue. We examine a novel approach involving transverse magnetic field-induced birefringence in gas plasmas to simultaneously modify the polarization state and increase the intensity of multi-petawatt laser pulses. Our findings show that a nanosecond magnetic field with moderate strength can effectively convert linearly polarized light into circularly polarized light, achieving nearly complete polarization alteration efficiency along with a significant increase in peak power. The technique's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical modeling, verified by experiments using low-intensity reference pulses, and the relevant parameters for full polarization alteration along with peak power amplification are clearly identified. We also demonstrate the potential of this technique to enhance the performance of optical parametric generation in gas plasmas. This novel method offers a promising way to overcome the limitations imposed by traditional solid-state optics in the development of multi-petawatt laser technology. Furthermore, this technique can be applied to other high-power laser sources based on different types of birefringent media, enabling the creation of extremely intense, fully optimized few-cycle pulses with modified polarization states. Rank metric and maximum likelihood decoding are both applied to correct errors that occur on the rank of a matrix, and this paper focuses on improving decoding for matrices with a specific symmetry property. It establishes an important connection between the rank of a matrix and the rank of a symmetric version of that matrix. Building on this connection, it identifies certain types of error that can be corrected more efficiently when the matrix has a certain symmetry property, and this leads to a new approach for enhancing decoding performance, especially for matrices with a high degree of symmetry. Additionally, this paper explores different aspects of its proposed decoding methods, including complexity, and it demonstrates its techniques with examples of symmetric matrices, parabolic surfaces of rank 3, and binary Ginzburg-Darwin matrices. It also shows that some of its proposed decoding methods can achieve a higher correction capacity than other methods, and it provides a general formula for calculating the enhanced decoding capacity of symmetric matrices. Furthermore, this paper discusses various applications and potential improvements to its proposed decoding methods, and it concludes with a note on the potential for further research in this area. In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a groundbreaking combinatorial formula for Pontrjagin classes, enabling the calculation of these invariant classes solely through the use of combinatorial operations. Their innovative formula, based on the heat kernel method, is equivalent to a specific integral formula involving the heat kernel. Our investigation delves into the underlying principles of this approach, examining how the heat kernel combinatorial formula yields the correct Pontrjagin classes. We demonstrate that the associated differential operators, derived from the heat kernel combinatorial formula, are precise, thus guaranteeing the accuracy of the combinatorial formula for Pontrjagin classes. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths, including optical, near-infrared, and radio. SN~2020jfo exhibited a Type II supernova with a short plateau phase, and our analysis indicated a high expansion velocity for the $H_\alpha$ line, approximately $3430\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, with a velocity ratio of $3430\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ to $1240\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ at 7 to 60 days after explosion. The spectral features of SN~2020jfo were comparable to those of SN~1999em and SN~2005ip at a similar stage, and our analysis of the absorption lines in the H$\alpha$ spectrum gave a black hole mass estimate of $1.5\times 10^{9}$ $M_\odot$ for the host galaxy UGCL-207. The metallicity of the host galaxy was measured as $0.16\,Z_\odot$, and we detected 12 distinct variable stars within the host galaxy using the All-Sky Virtual Observatory. The non-detection of SN~2020jfo in radio wavelengths remained unexplained, and our analysis suggested a progenitor mass of $11.0\,M_\odot$ $\pm$ $1.0\,M_\odot$ for SN~2020jfo. SN~2020jfo exhibited a distinctive early plateau duration of approximately 13 days, and our analysis indicated that SN~2020jfo followed the general development of SN~1993J. The analysis of SN~2020jfo provided valuable insights into supernovae with short plateau phases and the diverse characteristics of Type II supernovae. Implementing 5G antennas across a region is crucial for delivering 5G connectivity. Yet, little attention has been given to assessing 5G exposure among children and teenagers in schools and near hospitals. This article presents a straightforward, yet effective method for computing downlink 5G exposure around tower locations. We apply this method to analyze 5G exposure in major U.S. cities, including children and teenagers in elementary, middle, and high schools as well as patients in U.S. hospitals. Our findings reveal that on average, girls in elementary school are exposed to 12.6% lower downlink 5G values compared to boys, with similar exposures among middle school and high school students. In terms of absolute values, this equates to girls receiving 17.3 Megabits of downlink 5G per second less than boys. We also observe lower 5G exposures among non-Hispanic African Americans, Non-Hispanic Asians, and Hispanic or Latino students when compared to white students. In hospitals, our research indicates lower 5G exposures among patients aged 18-44 compared to patients aged 45-64 and above. These discoveries are meaningful, given the ongoing debate over potential 5G health effects and resulting calls for open discussion and data collection. As 5G is deployed worldwide, our analysis suggests policymakers, operators, and researchers should consider gathering more detailed information on 5G exposures and engage in data-driven discussions on potential health effects. In response to recent developments, we also update our analysis for computing uplink 5G exposure and provide adjusted results in the article's supplementary materials. Furthermore, we outline a suitable metric for assessing the uncertainty of computational exposure values. This article's findings and proposed method may serve as a foundation for more rigorous 5G exposure research, encompassing additional aspects such as side effects from combined 5G and other wireless communications exposure and statistical analyses utilizing more intricate geographical and demographic data. Ultimately, this research may inform strategies for managing 5G exposure, particularly in settings where individuals spend extended periods, like schools and hospitals. To address these issues, a novel sonar-integrated navigation framework was developed for indoor applications utilizing a layered control architecture. The framework separates navigation responsibilities into two distinct levels: a higher-level global layer, which ensures the robot maintains a desired course, and a lower-level local layer, which handles short-range obstacle avoidance. To mitigate sonar-related inaccuracies, a Bayesian signal model was designed to correct sonar readings, while a particle filter method was employed to fuse the corrected sonar data with the system's state estimate. The theory of contests has been the subject of various analyses in economics, however most existing models lack a mechanism for efficiently eliciting true effort levels from contestants. This paper introduces a new type of contest called the 'energy contest' where individuals exert effort in a totally ordered manner, and the payoff function is defined by an increasing and subadditive function over the set of efforts. The paper then provides an efficient mechanism for an energy contest with any totally ordered group of N players, and proves that this mechanism elicits the complete order of players' effort levels from highest to lowest. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that any energy contest can be transformed into a standard contest in a way that maintains the same order of payoffs for all possible strategy profiles. This technique allows for the efficient elicitation of effort levels in standard contests. Additionally, the paper explores applications for team contests and proves that efficient mechanisms can be designed for certain cases. This research makes significant contributions to the study of contests and order-based behavior. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have harder spectra. The study presented here aims to verify this hypothesis by comparing the X-ray hardness ratios of asynchronous and non-asynchronous polars using available data from the XMM-Newton database. The analysis utilizes the full dataset of asynchronous and non-asynchronous polars collected by Munott et. al (2020) and retrieves corresponding XMM-Newton observations for each target. The hard X-ray energy range analysis reveals a significantly higher hardness ratio for asynchronous polars ( $\langle HR_3-10\rangle=0.87\pm0.11$ ) in comparison to their non-asynchronous counterparts ( $\langle HR_3-10\rangle=0.43\pm0.05$ ). A two-tailed t-test indicates a significant statistical difference between the two groups with a p-value of 0.038. In 1991, Herman and Plotkin introduced the concept of normalization by evaluation (NBE) for typed lambda calculi, providing a semantic basis for analyzing the normalization properties of type theories. This technique has been the focus of recent research on the lambda cube, with multiple authors developing NBE proofs for various type theories. This dissertation explores the application of robust normalization, a refinement of NBE, to the calculus of constructions (CoC), a widely used type theory. Originally, the correctness of robust normalization proofs relied on the coherence of the context; however, this dissertation demonstrates how to modify robust normalization to account for the incompleteness of the context, thereby ensuring the validity of the normalization result for the calculus of constructions. Additionally, this work is being incorporated into the Homotopy Type Theory (HoTT) library, with the goal of affirming the correctness of the computational beta and eta equality proofs, as required for the HoTT foundation. Furthermore, this dissertation investigates the use of the refined robust normalization to prove the termination of the CoC typed gobini calculus, an extension of the gobini language with typing. Originally, the correctness of the termination proof relied on the context-to-term property; however, this property is insufficient due to the incompleteness of the context, resulting in the need for an alternative demonstration of termination. Finally, this research is being conducted in the presence of dependent types and the sigma (product) type, with the inclusion of a dependent termination proof for the CoC typed gobini calculus. The techniques developed in this research are also applicable to the extension of the lambda cube with dependent types. This lecture will introduce the one-dimensional Su-Hau-Yang model, a fundamental and easily understood topological model, and will use it to explain various complex concepts in topological quantum physics. Starting with the basic properties of the model, we will delve into topics such as the classification of topological phases, symmetry protection, and the implications of interacting with a topological system. A straightforward and intuitive approach will be used to make these complex ideas accessible to participants. As the understanding of topological phenomena is still evolving, the discussion will also touch on some open questions and topics for further research. Hands-on experience with numerical simulations of the SSH model will be provided to give students a practical understanding of these concepts. Applications of topological physics are vast, ranging from the optimization of semiconductor devices to the improvement of magnetic sensors, and thus understanding topological phenomena is essential for designing and operating both natural and man-made systems. The knowledge gained from studying the SSH model can be applied to other systems, making it a crucial starting point for exploring higher-dimensional topological models. The lecture will conclude with an overview of some exciting research projects that can be achieved by postdoctoral researchers. The goal is to inspire participants to use the understanding gained from studying the SSH model to make significant contributions to the field of topological quantum electronics. The lecture will cover the following topics: the basic properties of the Su-Hau-Yang model; topological classification and invariant; the realization of topological phases in systems with periodic boundary conditions; the unique properties of edge states in topological systems; the role of symmetries in topological physics; the simulation of interacting systems using the Su-Hau-Yang model; open questions and topics for further research; and the discussion of some exciting research projects. We examined how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts ion acceleration, focusing on the case where the frequency increase matches the ion movement. This alignment results in a key factor affecting ion motion - the laser's self-induced transparency - being maximally utilized, leading to more effective charge separation and enhanced ion energies. Calculations utilizing a two-dimensional particle-in-cell method showed that this alignment can boost the peak ion charge density by 10 times and ion energies by 100 times, compared to standard cases, reaching $10^{11} \text{ C/m}^2$ and $23$ GeV, respectively. This optimized scenario also enables the creation of high-energy ion beams with low divergence, suitable for future compact heavy-ion accelerators. Furthermore, this research indicates that a $10$ fs laser pulse can achieve the same results in much smaller scales, such as $6.7$ $\mu$m pillbox sizes and $d_0=1.2$ plasma focuses. These findings are displayed in the form of grid maps showing the dependence of ion acceleration on various parameters. Introducing a sharp cutoff in the laser field at $4\times10^{11} \text{ V/m}$ does not substantially alter these outcomes, demonstrating the robustness of this method, known as RIST. The underlying physics is analyzed through the renewal rate of the laser field and a new formula derived from it. This new formula provides a clearer understanding of the factors that contribute to this increased ion acceleration. Additionally, this research demonstrates that this RIST method is not exclusive to ions, as analogous results are obtained for the acceleration of background electrons by a similarly frequency-changed laser pulse, with the accelerated electrons forming a coherent electron beam with the same characteristics. This research is currently being expanded to multicomponent plasmas and high-energy electron production. The publicly available TOAST code, based on the open-source EPOCH code, is utilized for these simulations. Our analysis highlights the challenges of quantum field theory simulations, specifically for scalar Quantum Electrodynamics, when using qudits instead of qubits. Although increasing the dimensionality of the qudits improves the simulation, there is a noise dimensionality trade-off when using random unitary operations and parity measurements. We examine alternative noise protocols that leverage the larger dimensionality of the qudits, resulting in enhanced simulation results despite higher gate counts. These enhanced protocols include a combination of random unitary operations and four-level noise, which includes both depolarizing noise and amplitude errors, which we simulate on a quutrit (5-dimensional unitary) using the Homodyne-Parity noise protocol and find it yields improved outcomes in both the vacuum energy and mass gap simulations. These improved outcomes are achieved at a similar number of samples as the conventional protocol, which struggles with 4-dimensional qudit simulations due to overfitting. These results suggest that the enhanced protocols may mitigate the difficulties faced when using higher-dimensional qudits and could be applicable to other lattice gauge theories. Furthermore, we discuss the potential for these protocols to be implemented using a naive extension of the quantum circuit model and the challenges associated with implementing such protocols.
