This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS thermal detector, comprising seven transistors, for accurate temperature measurement. The design leverages a highly nonlinear thermal feedback mechanism to convert temperature into a uniquely proportional drain current in a single MOSFET. By applying a linear voltage ramp, the detector identifies the precise temperature at which the transistor's conductance matches a predetermined reference value. This reference value is established through characterizing the transistor's conductance at multiple, known temperatures to create a lookup table. The detection process converts the transient drain current into a corresponding substrate voltage, which is directly proportional to temperature. The design's effectiveness is demonstrated through the implementation of a prototype in a 180nm CMOS process, showcasing a tiny area of 2.26{\mu}m$^2$, minimal supply voltage range of 0.6V to 1.8V, and remarkably low power consumption of 100fJ per conversion. The design's limitations and potential areas for improvement are also discussed. The research explores ways to enhance the design's speed and energy efficiency, including the examination of subthreshold operation and custom ramp generators. The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. By solving a set of nonlinear partial differential equations, this method yields precise insights into a system's properties as its scale evolves. However, solving these equations directly is challenging due to their intricate and highly correlated nature. A proven way to tackle this issue involves discretizing the system using numerical methods, specifically the finite difference approach, which has been effective for solving a wide range of problems. In this paper, we apply this strategy to investigate the one-dimensional $O(N)$ model, a simple quantum field theory with a single variable representing the symmetry parameter $N$. By examining how the scalar field interacts with itself, we can analyze its behavior as the scale changes. Using large-scale computational resources, we have solved the FRG equations for $N$ ranging from 1 to 100,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000, and have made the results publicly available for download. These findings will facilitate further exploration of this model through the plotting of its equilibration diagrams. Similarly, we can plot the system's equilibrium behavior for different values of $N$, or, alternatively, the evolution of the model for different values of the symmetry parameter. This approach will also be shown to be applicable to higher-dimensional $O(N)$ models; however, these models require significant additional computational resources. The full source code used for these computations is also available for download. Furthermore, we have demonstrated an alternative way to solve the nonlinear FRG equations by integrating the discrete solutions over the finite interval, and have found this method to be accurate up to a relative error of $10^{-6}$. Music-based game development on standalone VR platforms like Meta Quest faces challenges, primarily stemming from the limitations of these devices to deliver high-quality audio via headphones. This restriction forces us to deviate from traditional approaches that rely heavily on auditory feedback. In response, we've created the Pied Piper game, which leverages visual and haptic cues to engage players in a satisfying musical experience within the VR environment. On the Meta Quest, Pied Piper challenges players to navigate a dark level, collecting treasure while avoiding enemies, all set to an enchanting melody that players must replicate by operating a pipe organ located in the virtual dark space in front of them. The game's sound is generated through a combination of the pipe organ's virtual notes and a background melody, which together create an immersive atmosphere despite the lack of clear, individual musical notes. As players progress through increasingly difficult levels, the background melody evolves, presenting a new auditory landscape for the player to experience. Ultimately, the game concludes with a thrilling boss battle, combining the elements of music, visuals, and haptics to deliver an unforgettable VR experience. The Pied Piper game has been designed to be accessible to a broad audience and has been successfully tested with players on the Meta Quest. Our research on this project is relevant to the VR music genre, and the techniques we've developed could be applied to other music-based games on VR platforms. The game's source code is available online, offering insights on managing high-priority audio on the Quest and the effectiveness of our haptic feedback approach. The Pied Piper game has been recognized at the IEEE Conference on Games, and the code has been shared at the IEEE Conference on Virtual Reality. The game's development has also been detailed in a chapter included in the IEEE Book Series on Virtual Reality. The project's source code can be found at https://github.com/IBranCunha/pied-piper and the game is available on Steam at https://store.steampowered.com/app/2132970/Pied_Piper/. This research provides a starting point for the exploration of machine learning in LiDAR point clouds, offering a unique perspective that could pave the way for more innovative data-driven approaches. In addition, our work is freely accessible on GitHub for anyone to build upon. In conclusion, machine learning holds immense promise for enhancing the interpretation of LiDAR point clouds, and we believe it is an area that merits further investigation and research. To investigate potential associations between neutrino sources and UHECR sources, researchers analyzed public datasets from neutrino detectors and cosmic ray observatories. The public availability of search tools is a significant step in facilitating such investigations. The development of new, sophisticated search algorithms for time windows and spatial associations is also recommended. The techniques and methods discussed in this study are applicable to multiple neutrino detectors, including IceCube, KM3NeT, and the proposed POPS and PTA components, as well as cosmic ray detectors like the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Askaryan Radio Array. The complex interplay between a liquid's surface tension and the roughness of the surfaces it comes into contact with determines the friction it experiences when moving over another liquid of the same type. While this interplay has been extensively studied for smooth surfaces, little is known about how rough surfaces made of texturized materials affect a liquid's viscosity. In this study, researchers created a type of surface made up of hexagonal patterns of liquid film and used it to show that the viscosity of a liquid film is significantly affected by these texturized surfaces, especially when compared to smooth surfaces. Additionally, they found that this increase in viscosity holds true even at very small particle sizes, at which point it is driven by the disorder created in the liquid's film structure rather than any roughness present. Moreover, this phenomenon was observed not just in soap solutions but also in oil and water mixtures, and it could have implications for how liquids move over other rough surfaces, especially those made of texturized materials, which are ubiquitous in nature and are used in many applications. In order to model this phenomenon, researchers developed a theory that takes into account the disorder created in the liquid's film structure rather than any roughness present, and it was supported by computer simulations of the behavior of the liquid film. In contrast to other types of disorder, such as the kind created by shaking, this type of surface has the unique ability to induce long-lasting disorder in the liquids that come into contact with it, and it does this through a mechanism called capillary elasto-dynamics that gives rise to the complex patterns that form in the liquid when it is placed on the surface. Understanding this phenomenon could also help scientists to learn more about the behavior of liquids in other complex environments, such as those with defects, and it could have implications for how liquids move over other rough surfaces, especially those made of texturized materials, which are ubiquitous in nature and are used in many applications. Scientists have identified the presence of several ethynyl molecules, such as cyanoacetylene and cylopropadiynil cyanide, in the TMC-1 molecular cloud. This discovery was made possible by analyzing millimeter wave spectra of the cloud using the Atacama Large Millimeter Wave Array. Ethynyl cyclopentadiene has been identified to exist in two isomeric forms, C5H5CCH and C5H5NCCH, with the former exhibiting a cyclic structure and the latter a linear one. The relative abundance of the cyclic form to the linear form has been found to be about 1.5 times greater for CCH than CN variants of ethynyl cyclopentadiene. This difference in structure may be attributed to the specific reaction pathways involved in the formation of these molecules. 

The total abundance of the cyclic CCH species, ethynyl cyclopentadiene, has been found to be about 0.43 times greater than that of cyanoacetylene in the TMC-1 cloud. The detection of these isomers provides valuable insight into the chemistry occurring within molecular clouds and the formation pathways of complex organic molecules. 

The analysis of the spectral data using the GALAXY package revealed the presence of two isomeric forms of ethynyl cyclopentadiene and cyano cyclopropadiynil at a frequency of 13.245 GHz, with an integrated intensity of 0.13 K km/s for the former and 0.07 K km/s for the latter. The detection of these isomers also enabled the measurement of their column density, which was found to be  (5.4 ± 0.7) × 10^12 cm^-2 for the cyclic CCH variant, (3.6 ± 0.5) × 10^12 cm^-2 for the linear CCH variant, (3.2 ± 0.4) × 10^12 cm^-2 for the cyclic CN variant, and (2.0 ± 0.3) × 10^12 cm^-2 for the linear CN variant of ethynyl cyclopentadiene. 

The present study presents the first analysis of the spectral data from the TMC-1 cloud at 13 GHz, a frequency previously underutilized in such research. This research demonstrates the capabilities of the Atacama Large Millimeter Wave Array in detecting a variety of complex organic molecules in a molecular cloud.

We further incorporate a focus module similar to existing models and combine the two for improved performance. Experiments reveal that our proposed look-ahead focus module achieves superior performance when tested on standard metrics and a novel focus-aware metric. Moreover, our proposed framework showcases robust performance under various attention-free configurations. This approach's effectiveness is attributed to its ability to mitigate the target-blocking issue and ensure the fluent expression of diverse meanings. The optimal detection of urban road networks using ridesourcing vehicles is a significant issue, particularly in areas with limited infrastructure. Ridesourcing vehicles, due to their extensive coverage and frequent navigation through urban roads, possess considerable discovery potential. However, their limited speed and frequent pauses between navigation segments pose a challenge. Consequently, the next important task is identifying urban road links based on navigation paths. Existing studies primarily utilize existing maps, road networks, and historical navigation data for this purpose. Our work is unique in that we aim to detect these links without the aid of these resources. We have formulated an optimal detection problem that prioritizes link discovery based on navigation path coverage. A key innovation is a novel characterization of the optimal detection problem, along with a cutting-edge algorithm called ROBIN, specifically designed for this challenge. Experiments using real-world data from over 1 million navigation trips in New York City demonstrate the effectiveness of ROBIN, with our approach outperforming existing baseline methods by approximately 15% in terms of covered reference links. ROINO, an optimized variant, achieves comparable performance to ROBIN while requiring significantly less memory. Furthermore, a scalability experiment with a reduced dataset showcases ROBIN's efficiency in optimal detection problems, with an approximate 90% reduction in running time compared to traditional methods. This work also explores the incorporation of a sensitivity parameter, which enables ROINO to prioritize the discovery of links that are more extensively covered by navigation paths. This is particularly useful in identifying links that are crucial for the overall network. The source code of our proposed algorithm is available online. Our work is relevant to various applications, including the development of optimal urban road coverage strategies for private fleet navigation. Additionally, it may be integrated with existing mapping services to enhance the discovery of urban road links based on navigation paths. This is particularly useful in areas where the availability of mapping data is limited. Our approach is adaptable to multiple datasets and easily integratable with existing mapping technologies. Deep learning-based automated emergency systems, like many other critical networks relying on artificial intelligence, are often deployed without their underlying mechanics being fully understood. Our analysis reveals that these models can enter into unstable cycles of signal enhancement, where they mistakenly amplify false information as genuine alerts. Additionally, we demonstrate that they overreact to valid inputs, producing an inordinate number of alerts for a single incident. We decompose the basis of this dual behavior into two key components: overstimulation and selective emphasis, explaining why it is challenging to prevent these excessive responses. Furthermore, we propose an alternative framework, known as the Dynamic Threshold Network, which addresses the issue of instability and overreactions in deep learning-based automated emergency systems. Our proposed framework achieves superior performance in comparison to the conventional approach, as evaluated through both empirical and theoretical analysis. Moreover, the efficacy of this model is showcased in scenarios mimicking real-world emergency networks, utilizing data sourced from Twitter. The code and model for this project are available at https://github.com/author/AES-UNICEF. Our analysis and model are relevant to any high-stakes, wide-spectrum classification network, like the UNICEF dataset, relying on artificial intelligence. The issues of instability and overreactions are inherent to deep learning-based automated emergency systems and cannot be rectified through traditional methods of evaluating and validating these models. The findings of this research are applicable to all deep learning-based automated emergency systems, emphasizing the necessity for the development of more robust, fundamental evaluation methods for such critical networks. The conventional approach to evaluating and validating these models as equivalent to human professionals in emergency situations is insufficient. The model proposed in this study outperforms the conventional approach in all evaluation metrics, underscoring the need for the creation of more effective methods for evaluating and validating deep learning-based automated emergency systems. In one dimension, a super-diffusive phase is identified and characterized by the convergence of an appropriately normalized local time sum to a finite non-zero value with probability one. This conclusion is based on the power tail condition being satisfied with an exponent between one and two. It has further been demonstrated that this phase convergence is markedly influenced by the size and location of the window of observation, and as a result, the normal convergence criterion of the local time sum does not guarantee the same behavior for all components of the local time. Instead, a stronger condition on the tail exponent is found to be necessary to ensure the convergence of individual components with probability one. The findings from this study build upon previous research concerning the power tail condition's effects on random walk persistence, and as such, they are established under the context of local time, thereby providing a new framework for the study of persistence in one-dimensional random walks. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate plasma features and validate the operation of plasma sources used in large tokamaks, specifically the W7-X stellar device. A helicon source is employed in IShTAR, where a hollow copper anode is used as a resonant cavity to generate high-density plasma. Recent improvements to the facility, including a mass-resolved q-meter and a Langmuir probe, have enabled precise measurements of plasma properties. It has been found that, in the helicon mode, the plasma density reaches 10^19 m^-3, with an electron temperature of approximately 3 eV and a neutral gas composition dominated by hydrogen molecules. Proton circulation measurements indicate a fast plasma recirculation, exceeding 10^8 m^-3 s^-1, which may impede the achievement of high plasma densities required in future stellar devices. Adjusting the anode voltage from -200 to -700 V results in increased plasma density but lacks the anticipated linear increase, and additional research is being conducted to better comprehend this relationship, aided by computational simulations utilizing the fluid model. Nonetheless, operating the helicon source at higher voltages has demonstrated the capability to produce high-density plasmas, and it is now being tested at the W7-X device. Furthermore, the development of a negative DC bias capability in IShTAR will allow for the examination of plasma features with shear flows, mirroring the conditions encountered in the divertor regions of modern tokamaks. This modification is expected to yield significant insights into plasma behavior and pave the way for the implementation of plasma sources in future stellar devices. This report outlines the progress achieved so far in operating the IShTAR facility and highlights the novel research opportunities presented by this test bed. In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit several advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and suppress insect populations. This system consists of competition equations describing the populations of nematodes, bacteria, and insects, along with external environmental influences. By analyzing and stabilizing the equilibrium points of this system, we derive mathematical conditions to prevent the spread of nematodes and bacteria through environmental contamination. These conditions create a mechanism to internally control the release of these microorganisms, ensuring the system remains stable and prevents the extinction of beneficial bacteria through excessive nematode reproduction. A numerical example illustrates the effectiveness of these internal control methods, demonstrating how they successfully suppress insect population outbreaks. Notably, our study confirms the potential of microbial pesticides to be an eco-friendly alternative to chemical pesticides, achieved through appropriate management of the microorganisms. Additionally, we identify and analyze the dynamic behavior of an unstable equilibrium point, further validating the efficacy of these microorganisms in managing insect populations. Finally, our study is a pioneering effort in the field of theoretical epidemiology, extending established approaches to research on nematode-based population management and highlighting the value of interdisciplinary collaboration between entomology, biology, and mathematics. By applying Lyapunov function methods and the center manifold theorem, we gain a deeper understanding of the intricate interactions within this tripartite ecosystem. Furthermore, our study paves the way for exploring additional applications and adaptations of these microorganisms in various ecological contexts. Finally, the straightforward approach used to internally control the microorganisms' release is a valuable lesson for other complex dynamic systems affected by external and internal factors. In conclusion, our study provides a compelling case for continuing research into the development of microbial pesticides as a groundbreaking ecological management tool. Along with the theoretical models used, the concept of control via microbial supression can be explored and adapted for use in other ecosystems and to tackle other pressing environmental issues. In the context of applied mathematics, the study of dynamic systems and their many practical applications, our work serves as an excellent example of a real-world problem waiting to be solved and the value of collaborating with experts from other scientific disciplines. While machine learning-based nucleus segmentation has achieved impressive results in recent years, inaccuracies in nucleus identification remain a persistent challenge. This paper proposes a novel two-stage convolutional network, W-Net, specifically designed to enhance nucleus identification. The proposed network is tested on a custom dataset of cardiac cell images and compared to state-of-the-art segmentation models, revealing significant improvements in both accuracy and precision. Furthermore, W-Net is adapted to accommodate multi-class scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness on a dataset of melanocyte nucleus images and highlighting the need for a robust nucleus pre-filtering process to mitigate over-segmentation issues. The proposed network is also evaluated on a public dataset of white blood cell images, showing its ability to adapt to new datasets with minimal retraining. The source code of W-Net is publicly available on GitHub, providing a viable solution for nucleus identification and segmentation. Experimental results indicate that W-Net achieves 84.4% accuracy, 87.5% precision, 82.9% recall, and 84.2% F1-score on the Cardiac dataset, 54.6% accuracy, 57.5% precision, 51.5% recall, and 53.4% F1-score on the Melanoma dataset, and 41.3% accuracy, 43.3% precision, 39.2% recall, and 41.2% F1-score on the NCL dataset. W-Net's effectiveness is also validated through comparison with state-of-the-art segmentation models, including U-Net, FCN, and Dilated U-Net. Additionally, the paper investigates the influence of nucleus priors on the network's performance, resulting in the integration of a nucleus prior filter layer that significantly enhances the network's accuracy and efficiency. The proposed W-Net framework provides a comprehensive solution for nucleus identification and segmentation, outperforming state-of-the-art segmentation models on multiple datasets. The paper's findings also provide valuable insights for the development of robust nucleus identification and segmentation methods. We examine the relationship between hamiltonian path index and the number of components in repeated line graphs. Specifically, we show that a graph G has a hamiltonian path if and only if its repeated line graph L^k(G) is hamiltonian for any k greater than or equal to 2. Understanding the intricate biological processes underlying pyroptosis is vital to developing effective treatments for this deadly disease. In an effort to this end, we developed a single-cell mathematical model of gasdermin D (GMD) ring formation and the execution phase of pyroptosis, leveraging available biological data to inform our model's parameters. This model highlights the critical roles NLRP3 inflammasome, proteases, and the actin cytoskeleton play in pyroptosis, revealing that treating COVID-19-induced pyroptosis may be achieved through the application of anti-inflammatory drugs, such as colchicine and auranofin. This work paves the way for the development of more complex multi-cellary models of pyroptosis, encompassing multiple cell types, in an effort to better understand the pathobiology of this inflammatory cell death and to design more effective treatments for the complications associated with COVID-19. Deep Neural Network structures, such as Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in recent years despite not being mathematically well-founded. Our analysis reveals that these architectures reflect standard signal processing concepts like matched filtering. Understanding the underlying mathematics of signal processing enables the creation of more sophisticated and general network structures, similar to GCNNs, which can be seen as a form of multi-scale matched filtering. Furthermore, our study shows that learning node features in an supervised learning framework is equivalent to applying a matched filter that is optimized for the classification task. Building upon this insight, we design a pre-neural network component that can learn and apply matched filters for feature extraction, which can be trained end-to-end as a conventional neural network. Our proposed method achieves superior performance when compared to popular GCNNs across various benchmark datasets. Additionally, it possesses the ability to interpret and prioritize semi-local information for each node, providing a match to the intuitive understanding of graph structures. Our research provides a foundation for the study of neural network components that are grounded in mathematics and signal processing. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengdian-li/mmf. In this research, accurate sub-pixel estimation of lateral tissue displacement in ultrasound elastography is achieved through the development of a novel estimation technique, called the Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA).  This technique leverages B-mode ultrasound data and a proposed source localization method to identify virtual sources of wave emission along the ultrasound transducer array.  By applying the synthetic aperture (SA) technique to the virtual sources, a VSSA image is generated from the estimated wave propagation time differences.  This technique was numerically validated and tested on simulated data, demonstrating root mean square errors (RMSE) of 0.048, 0.061, and 0.084 for in-depth, lateral, and through-thickness estimations respectively.  Further, VSSA was compared to conventional SA and sub-pixel interpolation methods on phantom data, yielding RMSE values of 0.21, 0.07, and 0.06 for in-depth, lateral, and through-thickness estimations respectively.  Additionally, VSSA was applied to in vivo data from a human forearm, yielding precise results.  This technique offers enhanced accuracy in elastography imaging.

Our key achievement is a data-driven solution, where we establish a theoretical bound for a first-order algorithm in clustering scenarios. We introduce a novel hierarchical framework for addressing complex nonlinear stochastic pursuit-evasion challenges, focusing on situations where one faster, fully informed agent seeks to capture a slower, uncertain target, aided by multiple slower, independently moving observers whose locations the target can manipulate. This situation is simplified through a two-tiered approach: first, the target's control is optimized within a inner layer; second, the outer layer identifies the globally optimal strategy for the faster agent, assuming it controls the target's faster component. This target component must be defined through its own model of the other agents' behavior. Our methodology is substantiated by an efficient algorithm and demonstrated with a representative parking lot scenario. Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images without additional X-ray exposure, thereby improving image quality. A popular approach called CycleGAN has been widely adopted due to its ability to perform non-invasive transformations between high-dose and low-dose images without needing paired training data. However, CycleGAN's performance is hampered by the requirement to learn two mapping functions and an identity function for both directions, which consumes more training data and complicates the training process. This paper proposes a simplified AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN framework that circumvents these difficulties by introducing an adaptive layer normalization switch, allowing the same baseline network to handle both high-dose to low-dose and low-dose to high-dose transformations. The proposed framework achieves comparable performance to the traditional CycleGAN while reducing the number of training parameters by approximately 50%. Moreover, it exhibits a notable 2-fold reduction in training time on a massive dataset containing 189,000 images. The code and model of our proposed framework are available online at https://github.com/zwang88/AdiC cycleGAN. For both the large-scale lung CT image restoration task and a smaller face CT image dataset, the proposed framework delivers cycle consistency results comparable to traditional CycleGANs. Experimental results on lung cancer detection accuracy and quantitative assessments of image quality also indicate comparable performance to baseline CycleGANs. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this limitation, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for dialogs, which incorporates semi-supervised contrastive pre-training. Unlike prior approaches, it groups dialogs based on underlying intents and axioms, leveraging both labeled and unlabeled dialogs for pre-training. Experimental evaluations on various goal-oriented dialog understanding tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. Notably, it achieves comparable performance to leading dialog datasets datasets baselines without leveraging additional datasets, and significantly outperforms existing pre-trained models on certain tasks. The proposed method also exhibits comparable performance to federated learning on small-scale datasets and significantly surpasses it on large-scale datasets. To study the rotational characteristics of exotic nuclei with broken symmetry, a comprehensive theoretical framework has been established using the angular momentum projection method onto the distorted ground states of halo nuclei.  A distinctive feature of this approach is the explicit inclusion of shape decoupling effects.  Employing a three-dimensional nuclear potential with central, quadrupole, and hexadecapole components, researchers have investigated rotational patterns in isotopes of $^{42}$Mg, $^{44}$Mg, $^{41}$K, and $^{43}$K.  A notable aspect of this study is the identification of shape decoupling phenomena in magnetic dipole transitions and binding energy patterns.  Additionally, this study enables the prediction of rotational characteristics in higher-spin states for experimental studies via electromagnetic transitions.  A key finding of this research is the existence of shape decoupling in the ground states of $^{42}$Mg, $^{44}$Mg, $^{41}$K, and $^{43}$K, which will be corroborated by theoretical predictions of monopole and quadrupole strengths, root-mean-square radii, and two-body separation energies within the framework of this approach.  Furthermore, this study suggests that $^{44}$Mg is an ideal candidate for investigating shape decoupling effects in rotational states via experimental studies of electromagnetic transitions. investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach through both
simulated and real-world experiments, observing significant performance gains in
multi-task learning scenarios. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/ayoosha/modular-mbrl. 

In more complex environments with multiple task switches, performance gains from
modular networks may not always translate to better performance due to the
increased risk of catastrophic interference. To address this challenge, we explore
the benefits of a soft-modular approach, where a single shared sub-network is
identified for similar tasks. The sub-network is assigned a higher probability
mass compared to less relevant sub-networks, based on the similarity between task
reward functions. By applying this approach in multi-task reinforcement learning
settings with extensive switching between tasks, we observe notable performance
gains in comparison to both traditional model-based reinforcement learning and our
initial modular approach. Moreover, the soft-modular approach enables us to
achieve a theoretical analysis of the representation benefits, further highlighting
its efficacy. The advantages of this approach are demonstrated through both simulated
experiments and a real-world evaluation on a complex robotics scenario, resulting
in superior performance compared to the baseline approaches. The code is available at

The problem of selecting the most informative points for an experiment or sensor network corresponds to a well-studied problem in mathematical literature known as the 'best subset' problem, however most existing approaches are restricted to linear models due to computational complexities. In some applications such as agnostic active learning and sensor deployment, equality constraints must be satisfied, either explicitly across subsets or implicitly within a specific space. This paper introduces a new sequence-dependent sampling algorithm, initially evaluating all possible subsets of points and then using this information to prioritize future selections, allowing for non-linear models and equality constraints. In simulations and real-world experiments with motion planning, we demonstrate that our equality-constrained algorithm outperforms existing methods. As a consequence, we also derive an efficient solution for the sequence-dependent sampling problem in linear models under equality constraints. In addition, we provide an active learning algorithm based on our method and evaluate it on images with varying constraints. Our work provides an efficient and general solution to the sampling problem, addressing multiple real-world applications. Code is available at https://github.com/nyu-mrl/seq-ses.

We tackle an intriguing challenge in solving inverse problems by estimating a hidden probability distribution $P_{X|W}$ given access to $P_W$. The key complication arises from the limited information provided by direct observations of $X$, which are linked to $W$ through the desired conditional distribution. The conventional approach, using maximum likelihood estimation, fails due to the limited utility of $X$ for regularizing $P_{\theta}$. We propose an unregularized conditionally trained generator as a more effective solution, utilizing a regularizer to make use of additional observations $X_n$. The regularized conditional GAN can be seen as solving an minimax optimization problem under equality and inequality constraints, which is shown to result in an efficient estimator with optimal risk at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(n^{-4p/(2p+d)})$ when the model is well-specified, outperforming previous methods. Moreover, we demonstrate the robustness of our estimator to heavy-tailed noise and its applications in image deblurring and denoisation. The theoretical findings are corroborated by Monte Carlo simulations and real-world image processing experiments. The implementation is provided in the publicly available code at https://github.com/zheng-wei-liu/RCGAN. 

In addition to the code, there is a associated arXiv preprint available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04198. 

We also present an efficient RCAN algorithm based on the BiGAN framework, which yields a faster optimization that attains a lower computational cost of $\mathcal{O}(nd)$ compared to the conditional GAN. The experiments on deblurring and denoisation indicate that the BCAN exhibits a speedup of at least one order of magnitude in terms of CPU time over conventional methods. The performance of the BCAN is marginally inferior to the conditional GAN but still achieves a relative error of less than $0.1$ in most instances. The theoretical analysis provides a minmax optimization perspective on the BCAN, which is an unconstrained problem under equality constraints. Although the RCAN can be viewed as an extension of the BCAN, we fail to establish an optimal risk for the BCAN due to the limitations of our analysis. Nonetheless, the experimental results validate its efficacy. The BCAN can be seen as an intriguing problem for future research.

This article examines the concept of stability through invariant surfaces in fractional dynamical systems from a mathematical perspective. We explore how the properties of Caputo and Riemann-Liouville fractional derivatives impact the existence and characteristics of these invariant surfaces. Specifically, we establish the condition for linear surfaces to be invariant in Caputo and Riemann-Liouville fractional dynamical systems, respectively. We also demonstrate that in certain cases, polynomial surfaces with specific exponential terms cannot be invariant. This research is an extension of prior works examining stability in fractional differential equations and provides a framework for analyzing the properties of solutions in fractional dynamical systems from a nonstandard analysis perspective. Finally, an application to fractional optimal control problems is briefly discussed. The answer to the question of whether invariant surfaces can exist in fractional dynamical systems is thus determined and the method is suitable for fractional systems described by order $\alpha$, $k\alpha$, and $1-\alpha$ for $0<\alpha<1$. Furthermore, the paper is an extension of a prior work on linear invariant surfaces in fractional differential equations and addresses the more complex case of polynomial surfaces. Next-generation wireless networks face significant challenges due to high frequency THz communications, which can lead to spotty channel estimation and degraded performance. To overcome these limitations, a new approach is proposed that utilizes reinforcement learning to optimize beam training in multi-hop communications. The proposed system divides the training process into two stages, with an initial coarse search followed by a more precise refinement process. The goal of the first stage is to identify the best big-beam candidate, while the second stage involves finding the ideal small beam. To tackle this two-stage problem, a dual-policy approach is developed, utilizing two separate reinforcement learning algorithms to manage the training process. The performance of the proposed scheme is evaluated through numerical simulations, revealing substantial gains over conventional methods. Notably, the results indicate that the proposed scheme can achieve up to 50% improvement in spectral efficiency and reduce latency by half. Furthermore, the scheme exhibits versatility, accommodating various channel conditions and training times. The code is also openly available for further exploration. The proposed system presents an innovative solution for optimizing beam training in THz communications, addressing key challenges and demonstrating the utility of reinforcement learning in evolving wireless networks. The research is also being explored to adapt this scheme for other cutting-edge communication technologies. The code is available at: https://github.com/zhengxiaoming2017/ML-THz-BT. High-sensitivity radio telescopes and wide-band receivers are expanding our understanding of the interstellar medium (ISM) beyond the local solar neighborhood. Scintillation analysis of pulsars offers a powerful tool for mapping ISM on a regional scale and has already yielded notable discoveries in several systems. This study utilizes wide-band receiver data from Parkes radio telescope to perform a detailed scintillation analysis of the pulsar B1133+16, which is highly distorted and bright. The findings indicate a high level of scattering and dynamic structure, likely resulting from the presence of a dense cloud along the pulsar line of sight. Additionally, time-variable scintillation patterns suggest the presence of an unseen structure, likely associated with a cloud at a galactic longitude of approximately 345°, which could be related to the Sco-Cen association. This detection highlights the potential of wide-band scintillation analysis to identify hidden structures in the ISM and shed light on the morphology of the interstellar medium on a regional scale. Furthermore, this study contributes to a growing list of regional ISM mappings, which can be cross-correlated with other observations to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the morphology and dynamics of the interstellar medium. This study also paves the way for future wide-band scintillation analyses of highly distorted and bright pulsars, which are capable of probing the interstellar medium on a regional scale. B1133+16 exhibits a wide range of scintillation patterns, including single-component, bimodal, and multimodal structures, which are associated with distinct line-of-sight lengths and orientations. This study further reveals the presence of an unseen structure at a galactic longitude of approximately 345°, which is characterized by time-variable scintillation patterns and possible systemic velocities. This discovery offers a unique opportunity to study the morphology of the interstellar medium on a regional scale, and future observations are necessary to gain a more comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon. Our proposed model builds upon the WaveNet architecture, incorporating a Pitch-dependent Expanded Convolutional Neural Network (PECNN) to capture periodic spectral variations induced by the fundamental frequency. During inference, a pre-trained PECNN is embedded in a QPNet to reproduce the original spectral features, resulting in a pitch-dependent generative model. Experimental results indicate that this model excels in generating music and speech waveforms with a range of fundamental frequencies, outperforming the standard WaveNet model. Furthermore, our model yields superior performance when compared to state-of-the-art non-autoregressive raw waveform generation models, as verified by structural similarity index measurements. This research presents a unique web-based annotation tool called MADARi, which caters to the complexities of the Arabic language for part-of-speech and morphological annotation, and integrates a spelling correction module tailored for Standard Arabic. This tool allows users to input original text and corresponding translations into English, leveraging Machine Learning models to predict Arabic morphological features such as base form, pattern, lemma, and part-of-speech. A spell-checking module is also incorporated to correct spelling errors in Arabic, leveraging a dataset compiled from a combination of sources including the Royal Academy of Arabic Language's dictionary, where available. This spell-checker is distinct from the typical English spell-checkers used in other annotation tools. MADARi's features include support for annotating single words, importing pre-analyzed words, and incorporating a thesaurus-based lookup for base forms. Additionally, the tool enables users to manage their own corpora and import existing annotated datasets in standard formats. With its comprehensive set of annotation tools and the integrated spell-checker, MADARi is an all-encompassing platform for Arabic morphological annotation and spelling correction. Furthermore, the tool is designed with user engagement in mind, incorporating an intuitive interface and an rewards-based system to motivate users to contribute to the development of Arabic NLP models. MADARi's annotation guidelines and data are openly accessible and tailored to standard Arabic, addressing the notable issues of diglossia and variation in Arabic texts. Two empirical studies are conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of the spell-checker, the integrated Machine Learning models, and the overall annotation tools. The results show that the spell-checker outperforms other state-of-the-art Arabic spell-checkers, with a 28% improvement in correction accuracy. Furthermore, the Machine Learning models exhibit a micro- F1 score of 57.6% in morphological annotation tasks, surpassing the performance of other Arabic POS taggers. The developed dataset and models are made available for further research and experimentation with the tool. MADARi is available online at https://madari.seas.gwu.edu/. The source code for the spell-checker can be found at https://github.com/AmrTawfeck/ArabicSpellingChecker. The annotation guidelines and data are accessible at https://github.com/AmrTawfeck/MADARiDocumentation. Colorectal cancer is one of the most deadly cancers worldwide, with its primary manifestation being a non-painful bowel movement. Although screening and early intervention are possible through colonoscopy, they rely on the expertise of gastroenterologists to identify and assess the severity of polyps. In this context, the development of an automated system for classifying polyps as benign or malignant would be highly beneficial, potentially improving the detection of colorectal cancer. Towards this goal, our dataset UniToPatho comprises 1026 H&E stained patch images of colorectal polyps, annotated by experienced pathologists to identify malignant areas, along with associated features such as polyp boundary, mucosa, and bleeding patterns. UniToPatho also incorporates a grading system for adenomas based on the number of high-grade nuclear changes, providing a comprehensive framework for the evaluation of colorectal cancer. This dataset presents several challenges, including varying lighting conditions, intricate tissue structures, and the presence of noise, as well as the complex nature of the grading task. UniToPatho is unique in its comprehensive nature, encompassing not only polyp classification but also a detailed assessment of adenomas, and is the first publicly accessible dataset of its kind. As such, it has the potential to contribute significantly to the field of computer-assisted colon pathology. We introduce a novel, high-order method for rapidly evaluating potential functions in two-dimensional spaces, specifically for applications involving steady-state flows. By leveraging an equivalent representation of the Green's function, we develop a computational technique to generate highly accurate approximations of harmonic functions in planar domains. This method, dubbed SwiftENS, yields a compact set of coefficients with clear physical interpretations, enabling several beneficial properties: fast evaluation times; seamless integration with discrete boundary conditions; and a context-independent format, facilitating adaptation to modified domains without recalibration. The efficacy of SwiftENS is showcased through an exploration of vortex dynamics and a simulation of turbulent flow, demonstrating its capacity for capturing intricate boundary patterns and generating precise, high-resolution velocity measurements. Furthermore, we investigate the potential of SwiftENS to model unstable states and Manson layers, and provide an open-source implementation of the method in the SwiftENS package.
